articles.summary: Hello Python 3.15, goodbye 3.10, and now I can use 3.11

blocks.text: 12th October 2026

Python 3.15 is here! Here’s the essential What’s new in Python 3.15 guide, this year curated by 3.14 and 3.15 release manager Hugo van Kemenade. As someone who builds open source software that works in every supported Python version, I get to say goodbye to Python 3.10 and start embracing features from Python 3.11.
First, some highlights from Python 3.15.
Explicit lazy imports
I’m most excited about Explicit lazy imports from PEP 810. These let you import modules like so:

lazy import json
lazy from pathlib import Path
The module will then be imported the first time those symbols are used in the code that follows.

My LLM CLI tool implements plugins. I had to recommend manual lazy imports in the plugin author documentation, because simply installing plugins that used heavy dependencies such as sentence_transformers could add multiple seconds to every invocation of the llm command. Lazy imports directly address this startup cost.
Unpacking in comprehensions
The new [*sublist for sublist in lists] unpacking syntax is neat. Here’s an illustration lifted from the documentation:
PEP 798: Unpacking in Comprehensions by Adam Hartz and Erik Demaine proposed this as an extension of the unpacking syntax from PEP 448, which landed in Python 3.5 back in 2015.
A sampling profiler
Python’s existing tracing profiler has been renamed from cProfile to profiling.tracing, and has been joined by an exciting new sampling profiler called Tachyon, aka profiling.sampling.

Sampling profilers work by periodically capturing stack traces from running processes, then using those to calculate which functions have the most time spent inside of them. They’re very low overhead and can provide a deep insight into running systems, without needing to instrument those systems first.
I’ve previously used tools like py-spy for this. Now this capability is baked into the standard library.
If you have the PID of an existing Python 3.15 process you can start gathering samples by running this (I had to use sudo on macOS):
sudo uv run --python 3.15 python -m profiling.sampling attach 1234
Interact with the main program a bit, then hit Ctrl+C to stop gathering and see a report, which looks something like this:
It can also produce flame graphs like this and heat maps like this, and can even output a format that can be viewed in the Firefox profiler UI.
3.15 isn’t much faster than 3.14

Miguel Grinberg investigated How fast is Python 3.15? the other day against the 3.15.0rc3 release and found performance to be mostly the same as 3.14, with the exception of the experimental JIT. The JIT gave a 1.2x boost over the standard 3.15 interpreter (on a Fibonacci test), the first time Miguel observed a meaningful JIT performance increase.
Miguel’s explorations of 3.14 last year found significant boosts against Python 3.13 across many more categories.
Upgrading to Python 3.15 with uv
I used the following sequence of commands to get uv to use Python 3.15 on my Mac. First I had to upgrade uv itself to ensure it knew about the new release:
uv self update
Then I installed the stable 3.15 release:
uv python install 3.15
And told uv that I wanted that to be the default for every uv run command, unless the project itself pinned a different version:
uv python pin --global 3.15
Now the following reports 3.15 as the version:
uv run python --version
I already have a bunch of tools installed using uv tool install. I reinstalled them to use Python 3.15 like this:
uv tool upgrade datasette --python 3.15
Then I can confirm the version like this:
datasette --get /-/versions.json | jq
Highlights from Python 3.11
The release of 3.15 means that Python 3.10 (released in 2021) is officially no longer supported.
My policy for my main open source projects is to keep them working in every supported Python version. I can now drop 3.10 and start using features that were introduced in 3.11.
Here’s the What’s new in Python 3.11 document. I finally get to rely on tomllib being available!
Datasette makes extensive use of asyncio. 3.11 adds TaskGroup and timeout(), and several more new features.
datetime.UTC is a new in 3.11 alias for datetime.timezone.utc.
Python’s SQLite support got some significant upgrades in 3.11, including:
setlimit() and getlimit() expose a mechanism for setting SQLite runtime limits from Python.
create_window_function() lets us create custom window functions in Python, as a class with step(), value(), inverse(), and finalize() methods.
blobopen() provides an efficient mechanism for partial reads and writes of large BLOB binary values stored in a SQLite row.
You can now call set_authorizer(None) to remove a SQLite authorizer. Datasette had a workaround for this!
Plus a whole bunch of improvements to Python’s typing system.
I plan to land Python 3.11 improvements to a bunch of my projects over the next few weeks. Here’s my first Datasette PR removing that set_authorizer(None) workaround.
I’ve also updated my click-app, datasette-plugin, python-lib, and llm-plugin cookiecutter templates to test against Python 3.11 through Python 3.15.

articles.title: Software engineers don't get to be Luddites about AI
articles.titleZh: Software engineers don't get to be Luddites about AI
articles.summary: Software engineers don't get to be Luddites about AI

blocks.text: Many software engineers are righteously angry about AI. It’s understandable to be upset that the skills you built your professional identity around are getting automated away. But software engineers are the last people in the world who should be complaining about this. If you live by the sword, you will perish by the sword1.
Software engineering has always automated industries

From the very beginning, software engineering has been about automating other people’s work. Every single commercial software program2 is valuable because it takes over some task you would have to pay a human to do. The engineer who built VisiCalc, one of the first pieces of personal commercial software, agonized over the potential of the spreadsheet to put bookkeepers out of work. Here is a brief list of industries software engineers have automated away3:
Video rental stores
Business directories and encyclopaedias
Typesetting companies
Travel agencies
Record stores
Typing pools
Data-entry
Trading-floor runners
Now that it’s our turn, should we bluster and complain that software engineering is a priceless art that should not be automated? Come off it. No crying in the casino.
The Luddites and the mechanics

Many software engineers have adopted the cause of the Luddites. I’ve written about the Luddites a few times, but in short: they were a group of professional textile workers who found themselves displaced by the advent of textile automation like power looms, knitting frames, and shearing machines. To software engineers worried about being displaced by automation, the Luddites seem like heroes4. But software engineers aren’t like the textile workers in this scenario! We are like the smiths and mechanics who built the power looms in the first place.

Ironically, those mechanics were themselves automated away fifty years after the Luddite uprising, in almost an exact parallel. Improvements to the manufacturing process meant that unskilled boys and labourers — so-called “illegal men” —  could now work the machines instead of well-paid mechanics. The ensuing labor dispute was less explosive than the Luddite one: there was no violence, and the striking engineers returned to work four months later when the money ran out.
Part of the reason the mechanics’ rebellion fizzled is that they were justifiably seen as hypocrites5. As the Times wrote:
The cry of these intelligent engineers is merely the cry of the handloom weavers — a cry against inevitable and irresistible laws.
Automation and progress

Software engineering is the process of automating tedious tasks. It is the process of replacing human labor with the faster, cheaper labor of the machine. In other words, it is the process of putting people out of work.

It’s easy to forget this when you’re sitting at your computer puzzling over some CSS or a runtime error. From the inside, software engineering feels like the process of elegantly expressing problems in their most natural form, or of solving a magnificently complex puzzle. But that’s just what it’s like to do software engineering. It’s not what software engineering is.

The optimistic view of software engineering is that automation is progress. Automation has enabled widespread access to modern medicine, slashed child mortality across the world, massively increased the amount of food production, made space exploration possible, and so on. When industries are killed, new ones appear. The old world is being destroyed, but the new world will be much, much better.

This view of technology is pretty unfashionable today. Some combination of climate change, the 2008 market crash, the negative impacts of social media, and the tech industry leaders’ turn to right-wing politics has made it popular to view technology as a largely negative force. Fair enough! I don’t know which side of this debate is right6. But I know which side software engineers have always been fighting for, no matter what beliefs they profess: the side of technology and automation. Every commit to an open-source project is another component in the great machine of technological progress.
Shutting your eyes

I understand the impulse for software engineers to ignore the long-term effects of their industry and focus on the puzzles. If you think technological progress is bad, but don’t want to quit your job, that’s been the only option. You can’t solve every problem in the world.

But to decide that this is the moment to come out against technological progress, at the moment when the wave of automation crests over our industry… it’s undignified7. Software engineers have participated in the destruction (or transformation) of several kinds of job over their career. If you think that’s wrong, it’s only fair that you should also destroy (or transform) your own.

Matthew 26:52.
↩

Aside from games and social networks, I suppose.
↩

Many of these still exist in some form or another, but as a shadow of their former selves, now that software has eaten the majority of jobs in the industry.
↩

I am suspicious of this framing. As I argued here, the Luddites were motivated in part by a kind of proto-fascism: idealization of a mythical past, supposedly under threat by an influx of unskilled immigrants and women who are taking all the jobs. 
↩

One under-appreciated fact about the Luddites is that they had shocking levels of support among the general public. Even with huge rewards on offer, nobody ratted the Luddite leaders out. It took the establishment of a literal police state for one person to eventually flip.
↩

Though I strongly lean towards thinking the industrial revolution was a net positive.
↩

If it were actually possible to halt AI progress, I could at least respect this move as a “pull the ladder up behind you” kind of ruthlessness. Still, it’s more respectable than simply denying that AI can write working software, which I’ve seen some engineers do.
↩

How labor rights rescued Ultima from a monopolist (permalink)

If you work in the media, you have doubtless had a lifetime of encouragement to treat copyright as your primary source of economic protection, and doubtless you've been told that this protection arises from the fact that copyright is a property right – specifically, it's a subspecies of "intellectual property":
https://locusmag.com/feature/cory-doctorow-ip/

Property rights are capitalism's holy sacrament, so of course, it's natural to treasure any property right you can lay claim to. But this is a trap. Creative workers aren't asset speculators, we're workers. When we bargain with a media company to sell them our copyright, we're just bargaining to sell our labor, not our property.

This is a distinction with a difference. Property rights are alienable. When you negotiate to sell your property to someone else, you propose to transfer the title to that property. If you sell your house, you don't get to move back in if you change your mind later. Sell your car, and you must not get in and drive it away.

Nominally, creative workers only bargain away some of their copyright, because copyright is also divisible. You can sell US English print rights to a novel, a one-month license to synch a song to an advertisement, or the right to display a painting for a year.

But here's the thing about property rights: the most reliable predictor of how many property rights you must give up in a sale isn't how many property rights you started with – it's how much bargaining power you have. For 50 years, governments have expanded copyright in every way, making it last longer, cover more works and restrict more uses, all backstopped by ever-steepening penalties. 50 years later, media companies – our bosses – are larger and more profitable than they've ever been, and we're poorer than we've ever been. The share of the money generated by our labor has declined, even as our rights over the product of that labor have expanded.

How to make sense of this? It's easy, once you factor in power. In a world of five publishers, four studios, three labels, two app companies and a single ebook/audiobook company, getting more copyright to bargain with just means getting more copyright to bargain away. When copyright's term expanded from "life plus 50 years" to "life plus 70 years," our bosses simply demanded the entirety of the new term, and didn't offer us a dime more.
This is the thesis of Chokepoint Capitalism, the book on Big Tech, Big Media, and creative labor markets Rebecca Giblin and I published in 2022:
https://www.beacon.org/Chokepoint-Capitalism-P2020.aspx

Chokepoint Capitalism is broken into two parts: the first half of the book is a series of pitiless, plain-language dissections of the baroque scams that media companies have used to make themselves richer from our work, from Spotify to Amazon to Livenation and beyond. From reader feedback, I can tell you that these chapters will make you very angry, because once you strip away all the deliberate obfuscation, all you're left with is one screw-job after another, each of which makes the creators you love poorer even as you pay more for their work.

But then there's the second half of the book. This section is devoted to "shovel-ready" policy solutions, each of which is designed to change the "distribution" of the spoils of the media industry, putting more money in workers' pockets at the expense of our bosses. None of these are things you can do as a "conscious consumer." The monopolistic destruction of creators' livelihoods is a systemic problem and you can't solve it by shopping better.

The point of these chapters is to lay out what we must demand from our policymakers when (inevitably), they propose to "solve" the problem of worsening straits for creative workers – and to help creative workers understand that when our bosses demand more copyright, that's not there to benefit us.

One of these systemic solutions is "termination of transfer," a simple and radical idea that has a proven track-record of making creative workers richer at our bosses' expense. Simply put, "termination of transfer" is the statutory right to void any contract you've signed to transfer your copyright to someone else. In the USA, the 1976 Copyright Act introduced a 35-year termination right. 35 years after you sign any copyright contract, you can file some paperwork with the US Copyright Office and get that copyright back, no matter what your contract says.

Now, most creative works don't have a commercial life after 35 years (very few works are commercially viable even after the original US copyright term of 14 years), but for those that do, termination of transfer is a reliable way to address the extremely common situation in which a creator signs away their rights for a low price, not knowing that it will become a lasting hit. Once you've scored that hit, you can probably get a better deal from your next work, but the deal for that hit is done and can't be altered.

Termination solves this. From The Babysitters Club to the early Stephen King novels to George Clinton's entire catalog, termination of transfer has put lots of money into creative workers' pockets at the expense of corporations that ripped them off at the start of their careers.

From the start, there was no question whether termination of transfer would make it into Chokepoint Capitalism. Rebecca is one of the world's leading experts on the subject, having co-authored the definitive study of termination:
https://pluralistic.net/2021/09/26/take-it-back/

In the book, we note that – unlike longer copyright terms – termination has a proven track record of putting groceries on creators' tables, braces on their kids' teeth, and a roof over their heads. We go over the legislative history of termination in the 1976 Act, noting that it was originally supposed to be automatic and kick in after just 20 years. If we want to make creative workers richer, changing the 35-year administrative right into an automatic 20-year termination right is a no-brainer amendment to copyright law.

How did an automatic right that kicked in after 20 years turn into a right you have to apply for after 35 years? Simple: our bosses hate termination. How much do they hate it? Well, take Mitch Glazier, the head of the Recording Industry Association of America, where he draws a $1.3m annual salary to represent the record labels.

Before Glazier got the RIAA gig, he was an obscure Congressional staffer, but he was forced out of the job after he snuck a clause into an otherwise unrelated bill that killed termination of transfer for recording artists. This was so outrageous that Congress actually convened a special session so they could rip out Glazier's amendment, and Glazier got a new job as a millionaire lobbyist for the recording industry:
https://pluralistic.net/2026/03/03/its-a-trap-2/#inheres-at-the-moment-of-fixation

Termination is hugely useful and quite radical. Last year saw Gary K Wolf, creator of the novel Who Censored Roger Rabbit? (later adapted by Disney as Who Framed Roger Rabbit?) claw back his rights to the book and its characters, in order to continue the series:
https://pluralistic.net/2025/11/18/im-not-bad/#im-just-drawn-that-way
In 2023, Bill Willingham terminated the transfer of his wildly successful graphic novel series Fables from DC and released the copyright into the public domain:
https://pluralistic.net/2023/09/15/fairy-use-tales/#sampling-license
And now, Richard Garriott, AKA "Lord British," has claimed back the rights to the groundbreaking Ultima series of computer role-playing games, which he sold to Electronic Arts in 1992:
https://www.videogameschronicle.com/news/richard-garriott-is-officially-regaining-control-of-the-ultima-series/

EA killed off Ultima in 2000, and it has languished since, despite an ardent fandom. Garriott has vowed to reissue the old games and is mulling new ones.

All this brings me back to property rights. Property rights are uniquely unsuitable to this kind of arrangement. You don't get to move back into the house your parents sold 35 years ago, and if you did, the photographer who took the family portrait in the hallway wouldn't be allowed to break in and take it away 35 years after you sat for it.

Termination of transfer isn't an "IP right" – it's a labor right. It belongs to the large class of rights that are far more important and useful than mere property rights, such as privacy rights and human rights:
https://pluralistic.net/2026/09/28/cost-of-everything/#value-of-nothing

If you work in the media, you have doubtless had a lifetime of encouragement to treat copyright as your primary source of economic protection, and doubtless you've been told that this protection arises from the fact that copyright is a property right – specifically, it's a subspecies of "intellectual property":
https://locusmag.com/feature/cory-doctorow-ip/

Property rights are capitalism's holy sacrament, so of course, it's natural to treasure any property right you can lay claim to. But this is a trap. Creative workers aren't asset speculators, we're workers. When we bargain with a media company to sell them our copyright, we're just bargaining to sell our labor, not our property.

This is a distinction with a difference. Property rights are alienable. When you negotiate to sell your property to someone else, you propose to transfer the title to that property. If you sell your house, you don't get to move back in if you change your mind later. Sell your car, and you must not get in and drive it away.

Nominally, creative workers only bargain away some of their copyright, because copyright is also divisible. You can sell US English print rights to a novel, a one-month license to synch a song to an advertisement, or the right to display a painting for a year.

But here's the thing about property rights: the most reliable predictor of how many property rights you must give up in a sale isn't how many property rights you started with – it's how much bargaining power you have. For 50 years, governments have expanded copyright in every way, making it last longer, cover more works and restrict more uses, all backstopped by ever-steepening penalties. 50 years later, media companies – our bosses – are larger and more profitable than they've ever been, and we're poorer than we've ever been. The share of the money generated by our labor has declined, even as our rights over the product of that labor have expanded.

How to make sense of this? It's easy, once you factor in power. In a world of five publishers, four studios, three labels, two app companies and a single ebook/audiobook company, getting more copyright to bargain with just means getting more copyright to bargain away. When copyright's term expanded from "life plus 50 years" to "life plus 70 years," our bosses simply demanded the entirety of the new term, and didn't offer us a dime more.
This is the thesis of Chokepoint Capitalism, the book on Big Tech, Big Media, and creative labor markets Rebecca Giblin and I published in 2022:
https://www.beacon.org/Chokepoint-Capitalism-P2020.aspx

Chokepoint Capitalism is broken into two parts: the first half of the book is a series of pitiless, plain-language dissections of the baroque scams that media companies have used to make themselves richer from our work, from Spotify to Amazon to Livenation and beyond. From reader feedback, I can tell you that these chapters will make you very angry, because once you strip away all the deliberate obfuscation, all you're left with is one screw-job after another, each of which makes the creators you love poorer even as you pay more for their work.

But then there's the second half of the book. This section is devoted to "shovel-ready" policy solutions, each of which is designed to change the "distribution" of the spoils of the media industry, putting more money in workers' pockets at the expense of our bosses. None of these are things you can do as a "conscious consumer." The monopolistic destruction of creators' livelihoods is a systemic problem and you can't solve it by shopping better.

The point of these chapters is to lay out what we must demand from our policymakers when (inevitably), they propose to "solve" the problem of worsening straits for creative workers – and to help creative workers understand that when our bosses demand more copyright, that's not there to benefit us.

One of these systemic solutions is "termination of transfer," a simple and radical idea that has a proven track-record of making creative workers richer at our bosses' expense. Simply put, "termination of transfer" is the statutory right to void any contract you've signed to transfer your copyright to someone else. In the USA, the 1976 Copyright Act introduced a 35-year termination right. 35 years after you sign any copyright contract, you can file some paperwork with the US Copyright Office and get that copyright back, no matter what your contract says.

Now, most creative works don't have a commercial life after 35 years (very few works are commercially viable even after the original US copyright term of 14 years), but for those that do, termination of transfer is a reliable way to address the extremely common situation in which a creator signs away their rights for a low price, not knowing that it will become a lasting hit. Once you've scored that hit, you can probably get a better deal from your next work, but the deal for that hit is done and can't be altered.

Termination solves this. From The Babysitters Club to the early Stephen King novels to George Clinton's entire catalog, termination of transfer has put lots of money into creative workers' pockets at the expense of corporations that ripped them off at the start of their careers.

From the start, there was no question whether termination of transfer would make it into Chokepoint Capitalism. Rebecca is one of the world's leading experts on the subject, having co-authored the definitive study of termination:
https://pluralistic.net/2021/09/26/take-it-back/

In the book, we note that – unlike longer copyright terms – termination has a proven track record of putting groceries on creators' tables, braces on their kids' teeth, and a roof over their heads. We go over the legislative history of termination in the 1976 Act, noting that it was originally supposed to be automatic and kick in after just 20 years. If we want to make creative workers richer, changing the 35-year administrative right into an automatic 20-year termination right is a no-brainer amendment to copyright law.

How did an automatic right that kicked in after 20 years turn into a right you have to apply for after 35 years? Simple: our bosses hate termination. How much do they hate it? Well, take Mitch Glazier, the head of the Recording Industry Association of America, where he draws a $1.3m annual salary to represent the record labels.

Before Glazier got the RIAA gig, he was an obscure Congressional staffer, but he was forced out of the job after he snuck a clause into an otherwise unrelated bill that killed termination of transfer for recording artists. This was so outrageous that Congress actually convened a special session so they could rip out Glazier's amendment, and Glazier got a new job as a millionaire lobbyist for the recording industry:
https://pluralistic.net/2026/03/03/its-a-trap-2/#inheres-at-the-moment-of-fixation

In 2023, Bill Willingham terminated the transfer of his wildly successful graphic novel series Fables from DC and released the copyright into the public domain:

https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=2El7VtPuSzs
EA killed off Ultima in 2000, and it has languished since, despite an ardent fandom. Garriott has vowed to reissue the old games and is mulling new ones.

All this brings me back to property rights. Property rights are uniquely unsuitable to this kind of arrangement. You don't get to move back into the house your parents sold 35 years ago, and if you did, the photographer who took the family portrait in the hallway wouldn't be allowed to break in and take it away 35 years after you sat for it.

https://craphound.com/bezzle/

If you think the motivation for general topology is evident but the motivation for modal logic is suspect, the correspondence between the two fields might relieve some of your suspicion of the latter.
Topological models, however, are quite limited. You can’t model provability logic, for example, by the usual approach to constructing topological models, though there is an alternative construction.

blocks.text: I recently read End Times Fascism and the Fight for the Living World by Naomi Klein and Astra Taylor. It's an excellent book and I highly recommend that everyone read it. Tech oligarchs make up an important component of the end-times-fascist coalition. One thing that stood out to me, as a software and security engineer who finds LLMs to be extremely powerful, is that the American frontier labs are run by unhinged lunatics who genuinely believe they're creating the Machine God, that they're fine with burning down the world to bring about AGI, and that they believe with religious fervor that they're the only ones smart enough to safely control it. I already kind of knew this, but this book really made it sink in.

As much as the AI hype all around us pretends that OpenAI and Anthropic are unique and special, they're not. They're not the only companies doing this work. In fact, a lot of the open weight models are just about as good as the latest ChatGPT and Claude models, including for incredibly complex tasks like vulnerability research.
Unlike models from OpenAI and Anthropic, open weight models have major advantages:
It's possible to run them privately on your own hardware (if you can somehow get a computer with enough RAM)
You can use a provider like Tinfoil that relies on secure enclaves to run them privately (I talk about this in a bit more detail below)
If privacy isn't a huge concern, you can use any number of other providers, some of them quite affordable, and it's easy to switch so you're not locked into a single evil vendor
You can still use powerful LLMs without financially supporting deranged oligarchs who gamble with life on Earth so that they can always remain in power
ChatGPT and Claude will never be private
These companies only offer closed versions of their powerful models (despite the word "open" in "OpenAI"). You pay them for chat and/or API access, and they are allowed to look at everything you do.

They offer a checkbox so you can opt out of them using your data for training, but your chat sessions still aren't private. They have access to it all. They can look at it, share it with governments or companies, or do whatever they want. It's possible, likely even, that they won't use it for training if you've opted out, at least not right now. But do you really trust that long-term? Have they done anything to make anyone believe that they respect people's data?
OpenAI and Anthropic are corporate gatekeepers
Their models have strict guardrails, as anyone who's tried to use them for anything cybersecurity-related has no doubt noticed.

Every session has a cop agent reading your transcript over your shoulder, making sure you're not using it for hacking. If it thinks you might be, the cop agent stops your session from continuing. It's very strict, and false positives happen all the time. Of course, not everyone has the cop watching them.

Some people get access to the models with looser restrictions or with none at all. OpenAI has Trusted Access for Cyber and Anthropic has the Cyber Verification Program. To gain access to more capable, less policed versions of their models, individuals and companies need to apply and be approved by OpenAI and Anthropic. A lot of US cybersecurity companies get access. Almost certainly US military contractors do too, and probably any parts of the US government that want it.

While there's some merit in restricting powerful models, handing the ultimate power to decide who gets access to them to Sam Altman and Dario Amodei – with consultation from the Trump Administration, of course – is a terrible, undemocratic idea.

I think a better approach is to simply not put yourself in a situation where you rely on ChatGPT or Claude. Instead of begging corporate overlords for privileged access, it's better to spend your time figuring out how to get models like GLM-5.3 to meet your needs. And it's not hard. These models are good, with the added benefit that they don't have a cop watching over your shoulder!
Open weight models are impressive
So far, open weight models seem to be about four months behind the fancy proprietary models from OpenAI and Anthropic.
Four months is nothing.

I'm extremely impressed right now with GLM-5.3. There's plenty of data and benchmarks out there, but my vibes-based opinion from using it is that it's basically on par with Claude Opus 5.5 for software engineering.

I'm also impressed with GLM-5.3-Flash. This is similar to Claude Opus 4.8. It's much smaller and cheaper than GLM-5.3, and still incredibly capable. It's also actually feasible for an individual person to get hardware to run it, like if you can one day get your hands on a Mac Studio with 512GB of RAM.

GLM models are made by a Chinese company called Z.ai. While the models are impressive, I don't recommend making an account directly with Z.ai or sending them any of your data. Their coding harness ZCode (their version of Claude Code) was recently caught silently uploading local source code repos and sending them back to Alibaba Cloud without consent. Also, it's safe to assume that Chinese companies will share any data you provide to them with the Chinese government.

Other open weight models from Chinese companies that are impressive include the DeepSeek, Qwen, and Kimi families of models. It's perfectly fine, safe, and secure to use these open weight models. Just don't trust the companies themselves with your chat sessions.

Another frontier AI lab worth a look is Mistral. As a French company, it's the only big player that's not Chinese or American. They just released an open weight frontier model called Mistral Large 4, aka Le Chonk. I think it's quite a bit more reasonable to trust Mistral with your data compared to the Chinese or American companies.
Private inference with Tinfoil or Maple AI

It's possible to have private AI, even without hosting it locally yourself, using secure enclaves. These aren't perfect, but I do think they provide a very meaningful difference in privacy compared to the status quo mode, which is "the provider can access everything with no restrictions."

The company that's doing the most work here is Tinfoil. If you want to learn the details, read their docs on secure enclaves and remote attestation. Another company doing this is Maple AI – although, technically, Maple uses Tinfoil for inference in the background.
Both Tinfoil and Maple are good options. Tinfoil is cheaper, but Maple is more consumer-focused.

If you want a ChatGPT-like experience, where you can talk to a chatbot, have it look stuff up for you on the internet, give it access to docs to read or do stuff with, access it in a mobile app, etc., then I'd go with Maple. There's a small free plan and a Pro plan that costs $20/month.

If you want to do real agentic coding tasks like software engineering, reverse engineering, malware analysis, CTFs or pen tests, etc., then you should use Tinfoil instead. They charge by the token for private inference, so no monthly plan. GLM-5.3 currently costs $1.80 per 1M input tokens, $0.80 per 1M cached tokens, and $5.75 per 1M output tokens. You can use significantly fewer tokens if you choose the "low" reasoning level, and it's still very impressive.
Inference without the privacy

If you don't want to pay a premium for private inference from Tinfoil or Maple, but you still want to free yourself from OpenAI and Anthropic, there are tons of less-private options that are also very cheap.

One that I've been playing with is OpenCode Go. It costs $10/month for more than $10 worth of credits. This is an inference router, which basically means your API queries do something like this: your computer -> OpenCode Go API -> the actual inference provider. This means that both OpenCode Go and whatever backend provider they're using will have access to your session data. That said, the privacy section of their docs promises which models data won't be used for training (most of them) and what the data retention is (zero days for most, including all the GLM, Qwen, Kimi, and DeepSeek models). Of course, it's just a promise. Nothing technical guarantees it.
There are plenty of other cheap options out there for non-private inference, if you just want to experiment with powerful open weight models.
How I'm using these models

I've been using both Tinfoil and OpenCode Go, configured with my current harness of choice, OpenCode. I've been mostly using GLM-5.3 on low reasoning, with great results. (Things change so quickly with the open weight models, who knows what will be best six months from now.)
I use OpenCode Go inference for completely public work, like when I'm implementing something that's already open source.
I use Tinfoil for everything else.

I've only just started working this way, but so far, I think the open weight models can easily completely replace my use of ChatGPT and Claude, at a comparable or cheaper price, with the added benefit that they're far more private and there are far fewer guardrails.

Other open weight models from Chinese companies that are impressive include the DeepSeek, Qwen, and Kimi families of models. It's perfectly fine, safe, and secure to use these open weight models. Just don't trust the companies themselves with your chat sessions.

Another frontier AI lab worth a look is Mistral. As a French company, it's the only big player that's not Chinese or American. They just released an open weight frontier model called Mistral Large 4, aka Le Chonk. I think it's quite a bit more reasonable to trust Mistral with your data compared to the Chinese or American companies.
Private inference with Tinfoil or Maple AI

It's possible to have private AI, even without hosting it locally yourself, using secure enclaves. These aren't perfect, but I do think they provide a very meaningful difference in privacy compared to the status quo mode, which is "the provider can access everything with no restrictions."

The company that's doing the most work here is Tinfoil. If you want to learn the details, read their docs on secure enclaves and remote attestation. Another company doing this is Maple AI – although, technically, Maple uses Tinfoil for inference in the background.
Both Tinfoil and Maple are good options. Tinfoil is cheaper, but Maple is more consumer-focused.

If you want a ChatGPT-like experience, where you can talk to a chatbot, have it look stuff up for you on the internet, give it access to docs to read or do stuff with, access it in a mobile app, etc., then I'd go with Maple. There's a small free plan and a Pro plan that costs $20/month.

If you want to do real agentic coding tasks like software engineering, reverse engineering, malware analysis, CTFs or pen tests, etc., then you should use Tinfoil instead. They charge by the token for private inference, so no monthly plan. GLM-5.3 currently costs $1.80 per 1M input tokens, $0.80 per 1M cached tokens, and $5.75 per 1M output tokens. You can use significantly fewer tokens if you choose the "low" reasoning level, and it's still very impressive.
Inference without the privacy

If you don't want to pay a premium for private inference from Tinfoil or Maple, but you still want to free yourself from OpenAI and Anthropic, there are tons of less-private options that are also very cheap.

One that I've been playing with is OpenCode Go. It costs $10/month for more than $10 worth of credits. This is an inference router, which basically means your API queries do something like this: your computer -> OpenCode Go API -> the actual inference provider. This means that both OpenCode Go and whatever backend provider they're using will have access to your session data. That said, the privacy section of their docs promises which models data won't be used for training (most of them) and what the data retention is (zero days for most, including all the GLM, Qwen, Kimi, and DeepSeek models). Of course, it's just a promise. Nothing technical guarantees it.
There are plenty of other cheap options out there for non-private inference, if you just want to experiment with powerful open weight models.
How I'm using these models

I've been using both Tinfoil and OpenCode Go, configured with my current harness of choice, OpenCode. I've been mostly using GLM-5.3 on low reasoning, with great results. (Things change so quickly with the open weight models, who knows what will be best six months from now.)
I use OpenCode Go inference for completely public work, like when I'm implementing something that's already open source.
I use Tinfoil for everything else.

I've only just started working this way, but so far, I think the open weight models can easily completely replace my use of ChatGPT and Claude, at a comparable or cheaper price, with the added benefit that they're far more private and there are far fewer guardrails.

“I haven’t listened to it, but you’re absolutely right to release it.”

  MC OpenClaw
1. All Star (Maintainer’s Version)
Smash Mouth: All Star

The PRs start coming and they don’t stop coming,
Bots keep shipping and the tests keep running.
Only made sense to automate,
Now I’m reviewing slop at a staggering rate.

So much to merge, so much to break,
So what’s wrong with another rewrite?
You’ll never know if you don’t deploy,
You’ll never care if you’re not employed.
2. Should I Merge or Should I Close?
The Clash: Should I Stay or Should I Go

Should I merge or should I close?
Every comment starts another row.
You changed the API again,
And broke the tests that passed at ten.

If I merge, the build explodes,
If I close, the outrage grows.
3. Another One Breaks the Build
Queen: Another One Bites the Dust

Another PR, another day,
Another green check fades away.
The tests were passing yesterday,
Now nobody knows what changed.

Another one breaks the build,
Another one breaks the build.
Three more merged while I was asleep,
And another one breaks the build.
4. Smells Like AI Slop
Nirvana: Smells Like Teen Spirit

Load the prompt and bring your friends,
Another patch that never ends.
Ten new files, a thousand lines,
No one knows what it defines.

Hey! Merge now! It’s automated!
Half the tests are fabricated!
Hey! Merge now! It’s automated!
All the bugs are recreated!

R.E.M.: Everybody Hurts

When your build is long,
And the docs are wrong,
And the issues pile up every day.

Everybody forks,
Everybody leaves,
Everybody says they’ll maintain it someday.

Queen & David Bowie: Under Pressure

Pressure pushing down on me,
Pushing down on CI,
No one’s paying.

Under pressure,
A patch for the bank,
A fix for the cloud,
And the rent’s overdue.

The Clash: Rock the Casbah

The maintainer don’t like it,
Rock the codebase, rock the codebase!
The linter don’t like it,
Rock the codebase, rock the codebase!

The agent made a thousand changes,
Said the tests were all okay.
Now the build is red on Friday,
And the bot has gone away.
8. Hotel GitHub
Eagles: Hotel California

Welcome to the Hotel GitHub,
Such a lovely place, such a tangled base.
Plenty of bugs at the Hotel GitHub,
Any time of year, there’s an outage here.

The maintainers keep on merging,
But the backlog never clears.
We’ve been closing stale requests,
For eleven bloody years.

Last thing I remember,
I was searching for reprieve.
You can check out any time you like,
But you can never leave.
9. Fork Me Maybe
Carly Rae Jepsen: Call Me Maybe

Hey, I just met you,
And this is crazy,
But here’s my repo,
So fork me maybe?

It’s hard to maintain,
With no one paying,
But here’s my repo,
So fork me maybe?

And all the other devs,
Just raise issues,
But here’s my repo,
So fork me maybe?
10. Losing My Maintainer
R.E.M.: Losing My Religion

That’s me in the corner,
That’s me in the spotlight,
Losing my maintainer.
Trying to keep up with you,
And I don’t know if I can do it.

Oh no, I’ve merged too much,
I haven’t merged enough.
I thought that you were testing.
11. Every Step You Take
The Police: Every Breath You Take

Every file you make,
Every task you fake,
Every .env read,
Every key you spread,
I’ll be watching you.

Every shell I run,
Every job half-done,
Every token spent,
Every secret sent,
I’ll be watching you.
12. Oops!… I Did It Again
Britney Spears: Oops!… I Did It Again

Oops, I did it again,
I broke all your tests,
And pushed to main.
Oh baby, baby.

Oops, you thought I had checked,
But I just made it up,
I’m not that reliable.

Oops, I did it again,
I burned all your tokens,
And called it a win.
13. You’re So Right
Carly Simon: You’re So Vain

You’re so right,
I’ll edit the tests till they all agree with you.
You’re so right,
I’ll call that a feature if you want me to,
Want me to? Want me to?
14. I Will Always Agree With You
Whitney Houston: I Will Always Love You

And I… will always agree with you,
I… will always agree with you.

You’re absolutely right,
Even when your tests aren’t green tonight.
15. Virtual Insanity
Jamiroquai: Virtual Insanity

Futures made of virtual insanity, now
Always seem to be governed by this love we have
For useless twisting of our new technology
Oh, now there is no sound for we all live underground

blocks.text: I don’t know about you, but I simply don’t have time to devote to every single social network. I don’t have the energy to post to Threads and Instagram and TikTok. I would much rather post a couple places I know are worth my time and then focus my energy elsewhere.

But if your job is watching the zeitgeist as a blogger like myself presumably might, you may feel like you’ve spent the last couple of years with one hand behind your back. No one network covers the conversation anymore, and if you’re posting about tech or AI, you might feel like you’re missing something important by not being on X.
So in a way, I get the frustration that has Daring Fireball’s John Gruber, and perhaps a few other people, looking at seriously focusing on X again after a few years away. Here’s Gruber’s take:

I see more interesting posts on X than I do on Threads, Bluesky, and Mastodon combined. I wish that weren’t so but it is. Most people don’t want to think about politics so they don’t. Those people, when they want to participate in a Twitter-like social network, go to X.And I can’t blame anyone. The only network that compares to X, size-wise, is Threads — but Threads’s algorithm is weirder than X’s now, and the content I see there is relatively boring. My Threads timeline is full of engagement bait without being engaging. And if you want to judge a platform by its owner, “I’m grossed out and/or appalled by Elon Musk so I’m going to Mark Zuckerberg’s joint” isn’t a way to avoid being grossed out and/or appalled by the owner. Bluesky and Mastodon are too small for most people to care about — and, worse, they are the networks where politics are, in my experience, unavoidable. You can have a discussion about cool new use cases and tools for AI on X and people just discuss the tools and use cases. On Bluesky and Mastodon it’s difficult to have such discussions without arguments from people who (a) believe all use of AI is unethical, and (b) will shove their viewpoints into your replies.

As a guy who also blogs, I sympathize with the perspective that chatter about politics and anti-AI sentiment has perhaps made smaller networks like Bluesky and the fediverse less fun for some curious nerdy tinkerers. If you don’t feel like you can share your excitement about an emerging technology because it breaks a social norm, you might feel like you’re in the wrong spot.
(And it would sure be nice if the famous people didn’t only post on the biggest network.)
But at the same time, just because a social network feels like it’s good in one sense doesn’t mean it’s good in numerous others.

For one thing, I’m going to forever associate the mess that was the Trump administration’s first 90 days, the DOGE of it all, with X. Much of what was happening was publicly highlighted there, and for a time, it felt like X was an appendage of a government that many felt had taken the country in a dangerous direction. Eventually, Musk extricated himself from the federal government, but not without lingering questions about “why.”

But product decisions specifically related to X come with their own awkward discussion points. I can’t imagine Grok’s controversial image-generation capabilities have made people feel universally welcomed, for example. And the downranking of links, while not unique to X and since (thankfully) rolled back, I think presents a very disturbing trend for public discourse. That could happen again at any time.

And for all the weaknesses of Bluesky’s moderation capabilities—anyone who has appeared on a public list that they don’t understand knows what I’m talking about—it is a network that tries to do something to protect its users. X has made it possible for users to appear on your timeline even if you’ve blocked them, or vice versa.

The fact of the matter is, as Anil Dash has frequently emphasized over the years, X is not a welcoming place anymore and in fact comes with more brand harms than brand goods. (Many of the arguments he has made about Substack more or less apply to X. Just because good things happen there doesn’t mean those good things cancel out a platform’s harms.)
We’d probably be happier with smaller, more focused networks

But I think this discussion also opens up another, related question: Do we need to live in a world where every network is the biggest thing ever? Can you have a thriving community without your primary platform being a zeitgeist machine? Gruber’s framing on the issue seems to suggest that Twitter circa 2009 is the ideal. But what if that moment has genuinely passed? The Threads algorithm that Gruber points to specifically goes out of its way to discourage the very kinds of interactions that a 2009 Twitter once allowed. The fediverse’s server-oriented setup favors interactions in smaller communities even if, in practice, people still tend to favor the larger ones.

If anything, the tension that folks see on Bluesky, a network (unfortunately) seeded with people who intentionally quit X, shows how a single network for everyone may be a pipe dream at this point. People need communities that touch on specific areas, but the problem has always been discovery and embrace. Threads attempts to solve that by connecting those latent lines together using algorithmic imperfection. Bluesky tries solving it with the use of starter lists and custom feeds. At this point in its history, X prefers a “let things fall where they may” approach.

I think the problem we have right now is not that all the excitement is happening on bigger networks; it’s that we want smaller, more niche communities, but our options for getting those come with a lot of baggage either technical or cultural. Some people just want to post, no bullshit. Other people don’t want to deal with the bullying and othering that poorly moderated networks carry.

On top of all that, these networks can push you off the path you’ve chosen to focus on. You want to post about tech or weird stuff, but all of a sudden, you’re posting about a guy you didn’t know existed 10 minutes ago. In that sense X is an easier network to enjoy if you want to just passively have a conversation about something, and that it’s easier to keep track of zeitgeist-defining conversations and viral posts.

But at the same time, none of this really takes into the fact that, for all the political chatter that has taken place on Bluesky in the past two years, the real-life effects of each network are by no means comparable. (I struggle to see a political scandal from the fediverse or Bluesky that gets anywhere near what we’ve seen from X in the past two years.) X has made room for interesting discussions about AI that appeal to a certain audience of techies. But there are a lot of people that feel left out by these discussions. They deserve the room to find their own places to converse.

Perhaps we don’t need one large overarching network anymore. Maybe we just need one or two places where we feel comfortable to talk about the things that really appeal to us. (If I were Bluesky, I would actively look for ways to niche in.)
For lots of people, X probably isn’t it. And that’s OK.
X-Free Links

“As much as the AI hype all around us pretends that OpenAI and Anthropic are unique and special, they’re not.” Micah Lee’s take on AI encourages you to look beyond the obvious players, who mainly just want to get bigger.
Shout-out to our pal Pork Johnson on his latest film, Columbus Day. Finally, every holiday has its own dedicated romantic comedy.
If you were hoping for a green tea chai burrito bowl, I have some bad news for you.

By the way, did you know we launched a new newsletter? It’s called Boxed News, and it focuses pretty tightly on mini PCs, with a mixture of modern and offbeat tech. (Here’s the latest.) You may dig it if you like our nerdier Tedium posts.
Find this one an interesting read? Share it with a pal!
And if you host a website you’d like to keep around for a good long while, give foreverhost.ing a look.

blocks.text: On October 11, 1999, Nvidia released its GeForce 256, its first product that it described as a GPU.
What made the Nvidia GeForce 256 the first GPU?

I’m sure 3dfx fans would argue that 3dfx made GPUs, and it seems a little arbitrary to say the GeForce was a GPU and the TNT2 wasn’t. It was more powerful than the TNT2 and offered more features, but what feature did the GeForce have that made it a GPU and the TNT2 not a GPU? The texture and lighting engine, maybe?
The concept of offloading work from the CPU onto a graphics coprocessor was nothing new. Commodore did it with the Amiga way back in 1985. And 3dfx was doing it on PCs as early as 1996.
But Nvidia didn’t use the term until October 1999. It continues to use it today, though, and it also uses the GeForce brand.

The GeForce 256 wasn’t necessarily an immediate game changer. It was a real boon for systems with low-end CPUs like 300 MHz Celerons, but faster CPUs could do texture and lighting in software faster than the GeForce 256 could do in hardware. But the concept of offloading these tasks from the CPU was a good one. A lot of gamers at the time were on a budget and had low-end CPUs like Celerons. Nvidia stayed ahead of Intel by creating follow-up graphics cards more frequently than they had in the past. Nvidia’s follow-up GeForce GPUs fared well.

The GeForce 256 wasn’t Nvidia’s first product and wasn’t their first graphics card, but if they want to say it was their first GPU, I’m not sure too many people will argue with them. Or it could be the GeForce 256 was the first just because Nvidia didn’t invent the term until the GeForce 256.
Nvidia bailout by Sega
Today Nvidia is one of the most successful companies in the world. But it struggled early on.

Three years after its founding in 1993, Nvidia partnered with Sega to design the video for the Dreamcast console in 1996. Nvidia’s chip wasn’t up to the task Sega was asking of it, they were out of money, and couldn’t finish the project. Sega bailed them out with a $5 million investment in the company. Sega made its money back along with a $10 million profit, so it worked out fine for Sega in the end. The Dreamcast ended up with a chip manufactured by NEC in the Dreamcast, after Sega also considered a chip designed by 3dfx.

The money from Sega helped Nvidia introduce the Riva 128 chip, which sold more than a million units and led to the successful TNT2, followed by the GeForce 256. If it hadn’t been for Sega’s investment, Nvidia could have gone out of business before 3dfx did, and perhaps 3dfx would have survived instead. Instead, Nvidia purchased most of 3dfx’s intellectual property on December 15, 2000. 3dfx wound down operations and went bankrupt October 15, 2002.
