Up until the 1960s, telephone calls were carried as analog signals. There was a
great deal of frequency division multiplexing onto open
wire, and
sometimes coaxial
cables, but in the
post-war period buried multipair telephone cables began to dominate. While the
network was surprisingly functional—long distance calls from coast to coast were
still quite intelligible—there were fundamental limitations to analog carriers.
The quality of the call would degrade with each step, a problem that was much
more acute for the sensitive digital connections that were already the apparent
future of the telephone system. These were digital signals modulated over the
top of telephone lines: the telephone system itself still handled them as
analog calls, just ones that required special care for quality.

During the Second World War, it became apparent that many of the long distance
network's challenges could be greatly simplified by using digital signaling as
the basis of the entire long distance system. In 1943, Bell Labs contributed to
the design of an early encrypted voice communications system called SIGSALY.
Unlike the "voice scramblers" and other analog techniques of the early phase of
the war, SIGSALY was recognizably similar to modern encryption. The voice data
was quantized into numerical values, so that digital arithmetic could be used to
encode it. In the quest to build a cryptosystem for voice, Bell Labs
incidentally built the first applied system for PCM digital voice transmission.
After the war, it was an obvious next step to refine this technology and apply
it to regular service.

This didn't necessarily mean direct digital service, at least not at first:
most subscriber loops remain analog to the present day. For the first years of
the digital network, even the exchanges themselves switched purely analog
signals. Between offices, though, encoding the analog channels into digital ones solved problems
from audio quality, to microwave path overloading, to flexibility in traffic
routing. Digitization became a core part of AT&T's concept of a carrier, just
like frequency division multiplexing had in the 1920s. That's the background to
the 1962 introduction of
T-carrier, the first digital
carrier in the commercial telephone system.
The Digital Hierarchy

Back in the article on T-carrier (which you should read if you are at all
interested in this topic!), I explained that T1, T2, T3, etc. are hierarchically
larger-bandwidth connections that carry the DS1, DS2, DS3, etc. digital signals
respectively. Let's quickly review this hierarchical concept and, just to keep
things interesting, add the further confusion of the D1 channel bank. A D1
channel bank is the physical piece of equipment that digitizes 24 voice channels
and multiplexes them into a DS1 signal, which will be carried over T1 carrier.

Similarly, four DS1 signals can be combined into a DS2 signal and carried over
T2. Seven DS2 signals can be combined into a single DS3 signal and carried over
T3. And so on, at least as far as they were able to get with the technology of
the time. The DS2 level maps generally to the D2 channel bank, but that
relationship can be confusing as the subsequently developed channel banks added
features as well as capacity. The D2 channel bank could multiplex 96 channels
onto a DS2 signal, but it also increased the overall quality of the audio
channel to meet the technical requirements for general mixed toll service (the
D1 had originally only been approved for conventional voice channels, not other
applications like data-grade leased lines).

In order to make that improvement, the D2 had to reduce the amount of
quantization noise introduced into the signal. The D1 channel bank had used PCM
audio with seven bits per sample, and calculations showed that eight bits per
sample would be required for a toll-grade connection 1. In a way, that
looked easy: DS1 already used 8-bit units. But the eighth bit, not used as part
of the PCM sample, was reserved for signaling purposes. No bother: the D1
channel bank hadn't really used the full signaling bandwidth anyway, so it
could comfortably be reduced to meet a compromise position. The D2 channel bank
used 8 bits for most PCM samples, but every six frames the last bit of each
sample was reserved for signaling use rather than audio. This created a slight
increase in quantization noise, and a significant decrease in signaling rate,
but the resulting numbers for both fell within acceptable margins. A perfect
compromise, but one that feels technically inelegant: in a sense, the D2
channel bank used 7.833 bits per sample. Ouch.

This must have given the Bell System's engineers similar discomfort, but the
aesthetic offense was worth it for backwards-compatibility. By the time the D2
channel bank was fielded in 1970, there were a huge number of D1 channel banks
and T1 connections in service. Backwards-compatibility to existing T1 lines was
a firm requirement. The D2 multiplexed 96 channels, four times a D1, and could
carry those channels over four T1 links—in fact, initially, this was only the
option. T2 and subsequent carriers were not fielded until after the D2. This
backwards compatibility provided an upgrade path, as well as a way to subdivide
the 96-channel capacity.

You might realize that it is also a completely alternate explanation of the
"hierarchy."

You might wonder why the multipliers at the levels of the hierarchy are so
inconsistent—24, 4, 7, 6. Reading the thing about signaling bits in every six
samples above might have stirred deep memories of a concept called "robbed-bit
signaling," a general concept of stealing occasional bits for other purposes
that was widely used with T1. These are all smells, indications that a system
was not architected, but grown. The "digital hierarchy" of T1, T2, T3, etc.
is not some elegantly-designed system, at least not nearly as much as T4-era
Bell Laboratories Record articles like to make it sound. It's mostly a result
of happenstance, as the history of the Dn channel banks shows: each new
channel bank, the D3, the D4, was designed to carry many more channels than
those before. They were also required to be backwards-compatible with the use of
the older channel banks and carriers. This process of exponential improvement
with backwards compatibility led to the digital hierarchy as a natural
consequence, not as a designed outcome.
Plesiochronicity

This emergent concept of layers of successively larger muxes explains the
digital hierarchy, but we now need to consider the problem of timing and
synchronization.

In any system based on digital sampling, you have to be aware at the point at
which those samples are taken in order to combine multiple signals. Consider the
scenario where several simultaneous phone calls are being combined into a single
digital mux for transmission. When the phone calls reach a D1 (or D2, D3, etc)
channel bank, it samples all of the inputs at an appropriate time to build its DS1
(or higher) output stream. Nothing about this case is particularly complicated,
except that it does require that all of the calls involved in the digital stream
are sampled under the control of the same clock.

But what about cases where lines need to be digitized in different locations?
Say you have two smaller offices in a city, that need to deliver inter-office
traffic to a tandem in the next city over. An obvious approach would be to
digitize the calls in each of their local offices, send them as digital signals
to one of the offices (perhaps the city's main downtown exchange), and then
combine all of those digital signals together to be sent to the tandem switch.
Doing this with channel banks wasn't very desirable: you would actually need
to convert the calls back to analog, and then back to digital, in order to
relay them from the first digital leg to the second. The first digital telephone
leads were like this: completely point-to-point, without the possibility of
switching or routing in the digital realm. That wasn't so big of a limitation
early on when all of the switches were analog and digital leads just made the
lines between them denser, but it prevented the construction of the fully
digital network that Bell Labs envisioned.

What was clearly needed was some sort of mux that could take four DS1s, already
in that form, and combine them into a DS2. Repeat this for the higher levels as
well, and you have the basis of a system that can combine and separate traffic
as needed to meet the level of demand between various offices. But what about
the sample timing?

If you have four DS1 streams from four different places, at least back in the
1970s, they are not going to be synchronized. The four D1 channel banks would
each be operating on their own sample clocks, and because of the imperfection of
the physical world some of these clocks would run slightly faster or slower than
others. When our four DS1 streams arrived at our notional multiplexer, the four
streams would be not only out of phase, they would actually run at slightly
different speeds.

We can imagine a lot of modern solutions to this problem, probably by buffering
relatively large blocks of samples in memory and then transmitting out of that
buffer. In the '70s, things weren't so simple: first, memory was expensive and
slow compared to the bitrates involved, and second, the latency involved in
such extensive buffering was not considered acceptable in a network that had
previously been all-analog and thus had no more latency than that implied by the
speed of light.

The solution to this problem, the Plesiochronous Digital Hierarchy or PDH, is
not easy to understand from our contemporary perspective. Many textbooks on
networking and communications make some nod to PDH, but it's often short and
cursory, and leaves you with a nagging feeling that the whole thing doesn't make
much sense. PDH is hard to relate to for two reasons: first, it was developed to
solve a set of problems that (due to broader technical advancements) we no
longer have. Second, even within those constraints, it is a solution that has
been obsoleted by newer approaches. PDH is not something that anyone would
design today, and in retrospect, it's probably best to think of it as a hack.
PDH was an interim measure, if you will, that bridged a gap between the
development of digital channel banks and the later development of a good
approach to synchronizing a digital network.

It would have been more convenient if those two systems had been designed at the
same time, but in practice, they weren't: digital long distance lines were in
common use a solid decade before AT&T had a reasonable architecture for a
digital network. You can already see that they were thinking through these
requirements in the late 1960s, leading to the concept of the PDH as a
hierarchical network architecture, but most of the actual technology to
provide that network was built later, in the '70s and '80s. For a while, there
was just, you know, something that worked. A duct tape fix. Conceptual bailing
wire.

So what even was the PDH? It is helpful to start by defining the word
"plesiochronous," which every textbook has to do since the term was invented by
Bell Labs to describe their design. I will spare the roots, but plesiochronous
means "almost synchronized" or "approximately synchronized." And that's what the
PDH was: it was a synchronous digital system with some slop. There was a little
wiggle room.

A DS1 signal is 1.544 Mbps, so if you multiplex four of them, you might expect
6.176 Mbps. You would be wrong: a DS2 is actually 6.312 Mbps. The overhead here
comes from the plesio part of plesiochronous. To understand how that works, we
should look at the design of the multiplexer from the beginning. AT&T practice
would call a multiplexer from the DS1 level to the DS2 level an M12, for, well,
multiplexer from 1 to 2. In practice M13s seem to have been more common
equipment, which were often implemented internally as seven M12s feeding one
M23.

In any case, the M12 takes in four different DS1 streams and then
bit-interleaves them, such that every 4th bit of the output is the next bit from
one of the inputs. This is simple to reason about and has the advantage that
virtually no buffering ever happens. But what if one of the inputs is running
slightly fast, and another slightly slow? The first thing to know is that the
output stream is intentionally slightly faster than all of the inputs. A
typical PDH system allowed a 50 PPM plus or minus variation in the rate of the
inputs, which means that the output had to be at least 50 PPM fast relative to
the sum of the inputs. That way, the multiplexer will never "fall behind"
because an input is providing bits faster than the output can interleave them.

The other thing to know is that the multiplexer must perform a function known as
either stuffing or justification. It is said that the term justification
was introduced within AT&T because it sounded more technical, while stuffing
was more popular with the actual engineers. Certain parts of each outgoing frame
are defined (by standard) as stuffable, and they're sometimes called gaps.
These are sections where the multiplexer is allowed to either include real data,
or to include some nonsense data called stuffing bits (or, if you want to
sound more technical, justification bits). By choosing to either include real
data or stuffing in the gaps, the multiplexer can actually adjust the "real"
output data rate up or down. That way, it converges onto the correct average
(the sum of the inputs) despite the "timing noise" of the inputs varying
slightly up and down in real speed.

If that didn't make sense to you, here's a different way to think about the same
thing: we can imagine the DS2 output frame as consisting of four "slots" into
which the four DS1 input frames are inserted (this isn't quite intuitive because
they are interleaved bit-by-bit, but the math works out the same). Under the PDH
design, these slots are all slightly wider than the input frames, so that
there is "free space" for the input frames to be shifted a bit in either
direction or stretched out. That allows the multiplexer to "catch up" on a fast
input or to "draw out" the frames from a slow input. Thinking about it in terms
of a wide slot that you can place the input into as desired also gives more
value to the term "justification:" you can shift bits around, or add extra space
in between them, just like you would to justify text.

The actual implementation of this idea is pretty complicated, because the
demultiplexer on the other end needs to know which bits were stuffed so that
they can be discarded. That's why PDH specified gaps at fixed positions: the
control signaling included a set of flags that indicated whether the fixed gaps
were used for data or stuffing. When the multiplexer decided whether or not to
use a stuffable bit (based on whether or not the input was getting ahead of the
output mux), it also had to store that decision for the end of the frame so that
the flag could be set correctly.

PDH wasn't an elegant solution, but it was a solution, and multiplexers were
designed up to the DS4 level based on the PDH approach. We all owe PDH a huge
thanks for providing the clunky stopgap that allowed the construction of a
nationwide digital telephone network. That said, well, it had quite a few
downsides.

First, PDH was never all that well standardized. Researching PDH is tricky
because there aren't a lot of documents that provide conclusive detail about the
actual implementation in the US, mostly just summaries, conceptual sketches, and
examples from Europe. As far as I can tell 2, Western Electric never really
offered a standalone PDH multiplexer. Larger integrated systems from Western
Electric (like, say, a microwave carrier equipment bay) might include a PDH
multiplexer, but it's not clear to me if WE even made them—the advertisements
and pricing information I can find for PDH multiplexers are from other vendors
like Farinon and NEC.

In North American practice, it doesn't seem like PDH was ever robustly
standardized, and there were implementation differences between equipment from
different manufacturers. That's probably one of the reasons for the scarcity of
information on PDH equipment: you wouldn't usually buy a single PDH multiplexer,
but instead would specify a specific model as part of a larger system. That
meant that the PDH network was far less flexible than AT&T had hoped.

The problem was even bigger when you looked overseas: AT&T tended to field
the best thing that Bell Labs and Western Electric could come up with, and then
promulgate that as a standard later on. The European telcos tended not to adopt
new American developments until they were mature, giving them the opportunity to
make standards before any equipment was in place. Thus the European versions of
US telephone carriers are often a bit better, and PDH is no exception. In fact,
the US, Europe, and Japan used three different hierarchies for PDH signaling.
The European standard put more channels into a stream (the "E1" at about 2
Mbps), and used a consistent multiplier of 4 for each level. European PDH
practices even got a complete published standard from CCITT. The Japanese system
used the same DS1 standard as the US but with different multipliers (4, 5, 3, 4
instead of 4, 7, 6). PDH could thus not be used for international calling
without completely remuxing everything.

Another shortcoming of PDH had to do with that remuxing. The decision to
bit-interleave the input frames together, stuff some bits, and then put flags on
the bit stuffing into the interleaved stream, meant that a PDH multiplexer
effectively "scrambled" the input streams. If you had, say, a DS3 stream and
wanted to extract a single voice channel from it, you had a lot of work in front
of you. It simply wasn't feasible with the electronics of the era to analyze the
stream to determine the interleaving and stuffing bits at each level. Instead,
you would have to put the DS3 through demuxers all the way back down to the
bottom of the hierarchy, pull out the channel you wanted, and then remux it all
the way back up. Pulling a single channel out of a DS3 could require two 11.5
foot tall equipment bays, and even further quantization noise due to the nature
of the robbed bit scheme.

Two things happened that pushed PDH to its limit: first, fiber optics. AT&T was
famously a late adopter of fiber, and 1970s documents on the digital hierarchy
talked about conveying it over T-carrier, microwave, and coaxial. We have
talked about coaxial
before, but L-carrier
was an analog system. Digital coaxial did emerge as the T3, T4, and T5 carriers,
but these were relatively short range and mostly only saw use on shorter
inter-office links.

Things were changing, though: by the time DS3 equipment was appearing in
telephone exchanges, competitors were already evaluating fiber optics. AT&T
dipped their toe in the water in 1976, with an experimental DS3 fiber optic link
in Atlanta. The next year, both AT&T and competitor GTE had DS3 fiber lines in
service (in Chicago and the LA area, respectively). Outside manufacturers
started offering T1-over-fiber equipment around 1980, and in 1983 AT&T had a
multimode fiber system stretching from New York to Washington. Sparing the
(fascinating) story of the business and competitive factors, the writing was on
the wall: fiber was the future of long lines. AT&T engineers realized that the
PDH design did not scale well to the enormous capacities that fiber could reach,
and even worse, that complex fiber networks would require exactly the capability
that PDH lacked: extracting single channels from the mux. Besides, despite the
systems in use, there really wasn't any standard for conveying PDH signals over
fiber, which only meant more compatibility issues.

Something else was coming over the horizon in 1983: divestiture. The complete
reorganization of AT&T in the mid-1980s, breaking the Baby Bells up into
independent companies, made the interoperability problems with PDH much more
severe. Bell operating companies (BOCs) would need to easily exchange traffic
with both AT&T Long Lines and, eventually, with other BOCs and competitive
phone companies and long distance carriers. That was very difficult when that
traffic was mostly conveyed in loosely-standardized black-box muxes. Many
aspects of US telephony were loosely standardized prior to the Bell System
breakup because AT&T ran the entire network and didn't really need to cooperate
with others. After 1984, the US became a lot more like Europe: for technology to
be widely adopted, it would need to have a well-defined, published standard.

That meant a standards body—the part of AT&T that had formerly published the
practices used by all of the BOCs, after divestiture, became an independent
company called Bellcore. Bellcore had an immediate goal of developing a fully
standardized set of digital interfaces to be used between telephone companies.
At the same time, a group of carriers and equipment manufacturers organized an
association to start an ANSI standards process for fiber-optic equipment. They
had a goal of an industry standard for high-speed digital fiber optics, so that
terminal equipment from different manufacturers could be used together.

That effort formed the ANSI T1X1 working group, titled Digital Hierarchy and
Synchronization. In 1985, Bellcore proposed their draft standard to the T1X1
committee: they called it SONET.
Synchronicity

First, I will briefly explain some context for my global readers. One of the
shortcomings of PDH was its lack of international standardization, and SONET
would not make the same mistake. Shortly after SONET was proposed to ANSI, it
was also proposed to CCITT. For historic reasons, and despite the fact that they
are largely identical, SONET (Synchronous Optical Network) is a North American
standard while the European standard is called SDH, for Synchronous Digital
Hierarchy. I will stick to the term SONET because it is catchier, but the name
SDH better conveys that SONET is essentially the same idea as PDH but it's
actually synchronous. Beyond that, it is also more feature-rich and much better
standardized.

SONET starts out higher up in the digital hierarchy. The "lowest" SONET level
is Synchronous Transport Signal 1, or STS-1, which is typically transported by
Optical Carrier 1, or OC-1. OC-1 operates at 51.84 Mbps, sufficient to carry a
PDH DS3 channel with signaling overhead. By this point in telecommunications
history, channel banks had improved and 50 Mbps wasn't what it once was, so
DS3 was a good choice for the basic unit of a high-capacity transport system.
This also provided critical backwards compatibility: DS3 was the most widely
deployed PDH signal, so by accommodating a DS3 within an STS-1, SONET provided an
easy route to tunneling legacy PDH links through a SONET replacement.

I put a lot of time into writing this, and I hope that you enjoy reading
it. If you can spare a few dollars, consider supporting me on
ko-fi. You'll receive an occasional extra,
subscribers-only post, and defray the costs of providing artisanal, hand-built
world wide web directly from Albuquerque, New Mexico.

By this time, the Digital Hierarchy principle from PDH was well established, so
SONET follows the exact same pattern—but, fortunately, the naming convention
improved. OC-3 is three times the bandwidth of OC-1, OC-12 is twelve times the
bandwidth of OC-1, and so on, with OC-24, OC-48, OC-192, and even OC-768 in
common use, the latter achieving over 38 Gbps of payload.

SONET is complex compared to what you might expect, or at least different. A
SONET frame does not consist of a header and a body. Instead, like with PDH, all
of the data is interleaved together in a way that feels messy. In an STS-1
signal, for example, a frame consists of three bytes of protocol overhead and
87 bytes of payload, making up a 90 byte pattern that is repeated nine times to
make up an 810 byte frame. Higher levels use larger frames but keep the same
structure, effectively mixing the header into each frame. Like PDH's bitwise
interleaving, this is done to manage latency: interleaving the header with the
payload avoids the need to buffer an entire frame of data at any point. Because
of this design decision, SONET can provide a latency that is less than the frame
time.

This description also oversimplifies by discussing only one part of SONET's
protocol overhead. There are actually several layers of overhead, all
interleaved together, that serve different purposes. The "lowest layer" overhead
is recreated at each regenerator along the route (devices that decode and then
reencode the optical signaling to compensate for path loss), while higher layers
are only processed by terminal equipment and are used for purposes like
connection quality monitoring.

These types of overhead are important because, unlike PDH, SONET provides a
specification for the entire physical infrastructure. SONET is virtually always
used with one of a few standard architectures, each of which are designed to
provide redundancy. SONET uses unidirectional signaling on the fiber, so any
SONET link will have two fibers normally active, one for each direction. Where
things vary are the approach to redundancy: in a linear route with automatic
protection, there are two "spare" fibers. When terminal equipment detects (via
monitoring protocol overhead signaling) that the connection quality is no longer
good on the primary pair of fibers, it will switch automatically to the
secondary pair.

Particularly common with SONET though, and particularly distinctive, are rings.
A unidirectional ring uses two fibers, one for each direction, but each of those
fibers goes in a circle and returns to the origin point. At the origin point,
each frame is transmitted both directions into the ring. The terminals
elsewhere on the ring compare the two copies that they received, one from each
direction, and use the better of the two. This provides protection against
damage to one of the fibers: terminals that are "downstream" from a broken fiber
should still be able to receive the frames that went the other way around.

A downside to this protection method is that it is inefficient: sending every
frame twice means that two fibers are still providing a theoretical maximum
bandwidth equal to the capacity of a single fiber. Bidirectional rings use a
more complicated monitoring scheme to detect when frames are lost, so that they
do not need to preemptively send them twice. A broken fiber will be detected
and, depending on the ring, either sent the other way around or sent on a second
redundant fiber allocated to the same direction.

SONET's ring architecture is one of its most interesting properties.
Unidirectional rings are often used as the "last mile" component of a SONET
network. Consider, for example, a large business in the early days of the
internet. If you wanted 100 Mbps internet connectivity, one of your best options
was to purchase SONET service from the telephone company. They would take an
existing ring, starting and ending with a telephone exchange, and figure out
how to add your premises somewhere along it. The ring shape allowed redundancy
with a relatively efficient use of fiber length.

Bidirectional rings, with their greater complexity but greater efficiency, were
usually used between telephone exchanges where there was adequate room for more
complex terminal equipment.

The ring topology also illustrates the biggest advantage of SONET over PDH.
Unlike PDH, SONET hierarchy levels keep overhead and frame data in the same
position, with consistent offsets to the framing data necessary to find an
individual channel. That means that it is practical to inspect a high-rate SONET
link, find a specific channel, and pull out those bits. You can even find where
a channel is located and then overwrite just those bits, inserting data into the
stream. This pattern is called "add-drop multiplexing," because the multiplexer
usually adds some channels and drops others.

Let's work a concrete example. Many years ago, I was an intern at a General
Electric plant in Virginia. Although the facility's main internet connectivity
had since been upgraded, SONET service was still active for redundancy and for a
legacy TDM PABX. In an equipment room, the telco-owned add-drop multiplexer sat
in a rack with the fiber enclosures where the building was actually spliced into
the ring. The multiplexer was the customer premises equipment, and our Cisco
router was connected by OC fiber to the multiplexer's "low speed" side while its
"high speed" side had two connections, one each way, to our "neighbors" on the
ring. The telco had left a diagram taped to the rack that made this material:
one pair of fibers went to the National Radio Astronomy Observatory, the other
went to the National Geospatial Intelligence Agency. There must have been some
interesting traffic on that ring!

The multiplexer found the time slots in the SONET ring that were assigned to
us, "dropped" them and sent those bits out on the low-speed side, and then
received bits on the low-speed side that were "added" back into the same time
slots. Each of the organizations along the ring did the same thing with their
own channels.

The fact that the SONET ring had to "pass through" each of its users was a
material downside, since a failure of an add-drop multiplexer at one customer
could cause service disruptions for others. That's why the multiplexer was
telco property, and further why SONET rings were always deployed with some type
of automatic protection and redundancy. Ultimately, though, a telephone company
technician still showed up at the security desk from time to time, needing to
perform maintenance or repairs on the SONET equipment.

The ability to perform add-drop multiplexing at any point on a SONET link also
enabled digital cross-connects. This, finally, was the original dream of the
nationwide digital network: by pairing two add-drop multiplexers together, you
can switch channels from one SONET line onto another, completely digitally and
with almost no latency. Paired with a management protocol called Transaction
language 1 (TL1) for remote reconfiguration, digital cross connects make the
long distance network vastly more flexible. Big chunks of long distance traffic
could be instantly rerouted, and consolidated onto major routes or spread across
more minor ones.

Now, you might wonder, what happened to the whole synchronization problem? The
most obvious difference between PDH and SONET is that PDH is plesiochronous
while SONET is synchronous. SONET requires that all of the terminals, at least
within a given interconnected network, operate in synchronization. That's
exactly the requirement that PDH rejected. What changed is the state of the art
in timing and synchronization.

A few things came together to obsolete the need for plesiochronous technology.
One was the introduction of the Bell System Reference Frequency: to coordinate
both analog and digital systems that were timing-sensitive, AT&T introduced a
nationwide time synchronization system. By the 1980s, the 2048 kHz Bell System
Reference Frequency was distributed to nearly all telephone facilities over the
long distance infrastructure. Various time code systems followed. During the
same period, GPS was coming online, and GPS receivers became a relatively
inexpensive source of precise time.

Most terminals on a SONET ring got their timing from the ring: they just
followed the signal and added or dropped channels at the appropriate time. A
"master" terminal, typically at the telephone exchange, had to maintain that
beat. In the early days, it would likely derive its clock either from an atomic
clock in the office or via a reference signal coming from another office. In the
later days of SONET, the time source was more likely to be a "BITS" or Building
Integrated Timing Supply. BITS are basically time servers for telephone offices,
typically using a GPS receiver as their discipline source and transmitting a few
different types of TDM time codes to whatever devices needed them.

Despite all of these measures, it's interesting that SONET still cheats. There
is a bit of wiggle room. Part of the SONET protocol overhead is a pointer that
indicates the offset within the frame that the payload frame actually starts.
SONET devices can thus start the payload a little bit late in a SONET frame,
providing an opportunity to fix timing errors. This capability means that SONET
is still an option even in plesiochronous environments, which eased the fairly
rapid transition from PDH to SONET.
SONET in Use

SONET is fast enough to survive into the modern era, although it is now
decidedly legacy. 38 Gbps is nothing to sneeze at, and still compares favorably
with a lot of common long distance connections. Where SONET shows its age is in
the actual network payload. What do you actually put on a SONET ring?

Well, of course, you can fit a whole lot of 64 Kbps telephone channels onto any
of the SONET tiers. You can do that using a "raw" T1 signal or via ISDN, which
uses the same basic fiber signals but better standardizes telephone signaling
(e.g. off hook status) and interoperability. But even an OC-1 has 672 channels,
more phone calls than just about anyone needs to make. In the 1980s, the driver
for commercial SONET service was data.

SONET itself is incredibly protocol neutral—one of the reasons for its unusual
framing structure is that it is agnostic to the size, rate, and timing of the
frames of the next layer protocol. SONET basically treats all connections as
opaque serial streams, so conceptually, you can put just about anything over it.

Because SONET evolved during the same period as ISDN, the two are closely
related. During the late '80s, as SONET was being deployed, the "Broadband ISDN"
initiative created Asynchronous Transfer Mode (ATM). ATM is a virtual circuit
switching protocol that multiplexes a large number of small, fixed-size packets
(called cells) over high-speed connections like SONET. ATM was, at one time, a
serious contender for the dominant protocol in wide area networks. That didn't
come to be, though, and IP took over—but not before ATM was well-enough
established to be a tempting way to carry IP. IP over ATM was fairly common, and
in fact, remained the norm for DSL until fairly recently.

There were other options as well: Packet over SONET was a standard for
SONET-based PPP connections, which could carry just about anything but were
often used for IP. A newer offering is Ethernet over SONET, which does exactly
what it sounds like.

The internet provided a compelling use-case for SONET, but it also became a
challenge. SONET was designed within the telephone industry, which emphasized
handling fixed-speed channels with very high reliability and very low latency.
The IP-based internet embraced the opposite: opportunistically moving variable
speed connections over relatively high-latency and low-reliability channels.
That meant that internet service over SONET became awkward.

For one, it tended to be slow. The reason was bandwidth allocation: getting time
on a SONET ring means getting channels assigned, and you will pay for those
channels 24/7 regardless of whether or not you use them. A technology called
virtual concatenation was developed to allow SONET's lower-level building blocks
(like STS-1) to be combined in arbitrary ways to produce just about any amount
of bandwidth you could want, but every Mbps over SONET was an Mbps that couldn't
be used by any other customer. You paid for it. Later on, variable-bandwidth
allocation systems were developed, but they were complex and missed the
opportunity to make much of a difference.

SONET's fixed-bandwidth design made it excellent for real-time media, the
wheelhouse of the telephone industry, but ironically real-time media was missing
from the information revolution. Internet connections were generally too slow
and unreliable to carry it. By the time real-time media returned, IP connections
had gotten so fast that they could make up for the lack of traffic engineering
with raw speed. Slow and reliable lost out to fast and unreliable almost every
time.

SONET also had all the typical warts of a telephone industry network
architecture. By the '90s, IP-based network equipment was both cheaper and
easier to use than ATM and SONET devices. Upstart internet service providers
were much more competitively motivated, driving down prices on non-SONET
services.

SONET has been superseded as a standard by OTN, Optical
Transport Network. OTN is an ITU standard for a digital hierarchy that starts at
2.5 Gbps and goes up, well, as high as you want. 800 Gbps "OTUC8" is now in
service. Besides being faster, OTN is also designed to accommodate variable
packet connections like Ethernet much more efficiently. And, of course, even OTN
is losing the fight against schemes that carry Ethernet frames directly over
fiber.

Is this the reason that 8-bit bytes became so universal in computing? I
genuinely do not know, this would be a good topic for future research. A long
time ago, on a different blog, I spent some time trying to establish the lineage
of the 8-bit word length that is now so universal. Without devoting a career of
research to the topic, I think the best I can say is that there seem to have
been several parallel paths that converged on 7 and 8 bits as good choices
for communications purposes. Digital telephony equipment was certainly one of
them.↩

And I would very much appreciate information from anyone who knows
otherwise.↩

Up until the 1960s, telephone calls were carried as analog signals. There was a
great deal of frequency division multiplexing onto open
wire, and
sometimes coaxial
cables, but in the
post-war period buried multipair telephone cables began to dominate. While the
network was surprisingly functional—long distance calls from coast to coast were
still quite intelligible—there were fundamental limitations to analog carriers.
The quality of the call would degrade with each step, a problem that was much
more acute for the sensitive digital connections that were already the apparent
future of the telephone system. These were digital signals modulated over the
top of telephone lines: the telephone system itself still handled them as
analog calls, just ones that required special care for quality.

During the Second World War, it became apparent that many of the long distance
network's challenges could be greatly simplified by using digital signaling as
the basis of the entire long distance system. In 1943, Bell Labs contributed to
the design of an early encrypted voice communications system called SIGSALY.
Unlike the "voice scramblers" and other analog techniques of the early phase of
the war, SIGSALY was recognizably similar to modern encryption. The voice data
was quantized into numerical values, so that digital arithmetic could be used to
encode it. In the quest to build a cryptosystem for voice, Bell Labs
incidentally built the first applied system for PCM digital voice transmission.
After the war, it was an obvious next step to refine this technology and apply
it to regular service.

This didn't necessarily mean direct digital service, at least not at first:
most subscriber loops remain analog to the present day. For the first years of
the digital network, even the exchanges themselves switched purely analog
signals. Between offices, though, encoding the analog channels into digital ones solved problems
from audio quality, to microwave path overloading, to flexibility in traffic
routing. Digitization became a core part of AT&T's concept of a carrier, just
like frequency division multiplexing had in the 1920s. That's the background to
the 1962 introduction of
T-carrier, the first digital
carrier in the commercial telephone system.
The Digital Hierarchy

Back in the article on T-carrier (which you should read if you are at all
interested in this topic!), I explained that T1, T2, T3, etc. are hierarchically
larger-bandwidth connections that carry the DS1, DS2, DS3, etc. digital signals
respectively. Let's quickly review this hierarchical concept and, just to keep
things interesting, add the further confusion of the D1 channel bank. A D1
channel bank is the physical piece of equipment that digitizes 24 voice channels
and multiplexes them into a DS1 signal, which will be carried over T1 carrier.

Similarly, four DS1 signals can be combined into a DS2 signal and carried over
T2. Seven DS2 signals can be combined into a single DS3 signal and carried over
T3. And so on, at least as far as they were able to get with the technology of
the time. The DS2 level maps generally to the D2 channel bank, but that
relationship can be confusing as the subsequently developed channel banks added
features as well as capacity. The D2 channel bank could multiplex 96 channels
onto a DS2 signal, but it also increased the overall quality of the audio
channel to meet the technical requirements for general mixed toll service (the
D1 had originally only been approved for conventional voice channels, not other
applications like data-grade leased lines).

In order to make that improvement, the D2 had to reduce the amount of
quantization noise introduced into the signal. The D1 channel bank had used PCM
audio with seven bits per sample, and calculations showed that eight bits per
sample would be required for a toll-grade connection 1. In a way, that
looked easy: DS1 already used 8-bit units. But the eighth bit, not used as part
of the PCM sample, was reserved for signaling purposes. No bother: the D1
channel bank hadn't really used the full signaling bandwidth anyway, so it
could comfortably be reduced to meet a compromise position. The D2 channel bank
used 8 bits for most PCM samples, but every six frames the last bit of each
sample was reserved for signaling use rather than audio. This created a slight
increase in quantization noise, and a significant decrease in signaling rate,
but the resulting numbers for both fell within acceptable margins. A perfect
compromise, but one that feels technically inelegant: in a sense, the D2
channel bank used 7.833 bits per sample. Ouch.

This must have given the Bell System's engineers similar discomfort, but the
aesthetic offense was worth it for backwards-compatibility. By the time the D2
channel bank was fielded in 1970, there were a huge number of D1 channel banks
and T1 connections in service. Backwards-compatibility to existing T1 lines was
a firm requirement. The D2 multiplexed 96 channels, four times a D1, and could
carry those channels over four T1 links—in fact, initially, this was only the
option. T2 and subsequent carriers were not fielded until after the D2. This
backwards compatibility provided an upgrade path, as well as a way to subdivide
the 96-channel capacity.

You might realize that it is also a completely alternate explanation of the
"hierarchy."

You might wonder why the multipliers at the levels of the hierarchy are so
inconsistent—24, 4, 7, 6. Reading the thing about signaling bits in every six
samples above might have stirred deep memories of a concept called "robbed-bit
signaling," a general concept of stealing occasional bits for other purposes
that was widely used with T1. These are all smells, indications that a system
was not architected, but grown. The "digital hierarchy" of T1, T2, T3, etc.
is not some elegantly-designed system, at least not nearly as much as T4-era
Bell Laboratories Record articles like to make it sound. It's mostly a result
of happenstance, as the history of the Dn channel banks shows: each new
channel bank, the D3, the D4, was designed to carry many more channels than
those before. They were also required to be backwards-compatible with the use of
the older channel banks and carriers. This process of exponential improvement
with backwards compatibility led to the digital hierarchy as a natural
consequence, not as a designed outcome.
Plesiochronicity

This emergent concept of layers of successively larger muxes explains the
digital hierarchy, but we now need to consider the problem of timing and
synchronization.

In any system based on digital sampling, you have to be aware at the point at
which those samples are taken in order to combine multiple signals. Consider the
scenario where several simultaneous phone calls are being combined into a single
digital mux for transmission. When the phone calls reach a D1 (or D2, D3, etc)
channel bank, it samples all of the inputs at an appropriate time to build its DS1
(or higher) output stream. Nothing about this case is particularly complicated,
except that it does require that all of the calls involved in the digital stream
are sampled under the control of the same clock.

But what about cases where lines need to be digitized in different locations?
Say you have two smaller offices in a city, that need to deliver inter-office
traffic to a tandem in the next city over. An obvious approach would be to
digitize the calls in each of their local offices, send them as digital signals
to one of the offices (perhaps the city's main downtown exchange), and then
combine all of those digital signals together to be sent to the tandem switch.
Doing this with channel banks wasn't very desirable: you would actually need
to convert the calls back to analog, and then back to digital, in order to
relay them from the first digital leg to the second. The first digital telephone
leads were like this: completely point-to-point, without the possibility of
switching or routing in the digital realm. That wasn't so big of a limitation
early on when all of the switches were analog and digital leads just made the
lines between them denser, but it prevented the construction of the fully
digital network that Bell Labs envisioned.

What was clearly needed was some sort of mux that could take four DS1s, already
in that form, and combine them into a DS2. Repeat this for the higher levels as
well, and you have the basis of a system that can combine and separate traffic
as needed to meet the level of demand between various offices. But what about
the sample timing?

If you have four DS1 streams from four different places, at least back in the
1970s, they are not going to be synchronized. The four D1 channel banks would
each be operating on their own sample clocks, and because of the imperfection of
the physical world some of these clocks would run slightly faster or slower than
others. When our four DS1 streams arrived at our notional multiplexer, the four
streams would be not only out of phase, they would actually run at slightly
different speeds.

We can imagine a lot of modern solutions to this problem, probably by buffering
relatively large blocks of samples in memory and then transmitting out of that
buffer. In the '70s, things weren't so simple: first, memory was expensive and
slow compared to the bitrates involved, and second, the latency involved in
such extensive buffering was not considered acceptable in a network that had
previously been all-analog and thus had no more latency than that implied by the
speed of light.

The solution to this problem, the Plesiochronous Digital Hierarchy or PDH, is
not easy to understand from our contemporary perspective. Many textbooks on
networking and communications make some nod to PDH, but it's often short and
cursory, and leaves you with a nagging feeling that the whole thing doesn't make
much sense. PDH is hard to relate to for two reasons: first, it was developed to
solve a set of problems that (due to broader technical advancements) we no
longer have. Second, even within those constraints, it is a solution that has
been obsoleted by newer approaches. PDH is not something that anyone would
design today, and in retrospect, it's probably best to think of it as a hack.
PDH was an interim measure, if you will, that bridged a gap between the
development of digital channel banks and the later development of a good
approach to synchronizing a digital network.

It would have been more convenient if those two systems had been designed at the
same time, but in practice, they weren't: digital long distance lines were in
common use a solid decade before AT&T had a reasonable architecture for a
digital network. You can already see that they were thinking through these
requirements in the late 1960s, leading to the concept of the PDH as a
hierarchical network architecture, but most of the actual technology to
provide that network was built later, in the '70s and '80s. For a while, there
was just, you know, something that worked. A duct tape fix. Conceptual bailing
wire.

So what even was the PDH? It is helpful to start by defining the word
"plesiochronous," which every textbook has to do since the term was invented by
Bell Labs to describe their design. I will spare the roots, but plesiochronous
means "almost synchronized" or "approximately synchronized." And that's what the
PDH was: it was a synchronous digital system with some slop. There was a little
wiggle room.

A DS1 signal is 1.544 Mbps, so if you multiplex four of them, you might expect
6.176 Mbps. You would be wrong: a DS2 is actually 6.312 Mbps. The overhead here
comes from the plesio part of plesiochronous. To understand how that works, we
should look at the design of the multiplexer from the beginning. AT&T practice
would call a multiplexer from the DS1 level to the DS2 level an M12, for, well,
multiplexer from 1 to 2. In practice M13s seem to have been more common
equipment, which were often implemented internally as seven M12s feeding one
M23.

In any case, the M12 takes in four different DS1 streams and then
bit-interleaves them, such that every 4th bit of the output is the next bit from
one of the inputs. This is simple to reason about and has the advantage that
virtually no buffering ever happens. But what if one of the inputs is running
slightly fast, and another slightly slow? The first thing to know is that the
output stream is intentionally slightly faster than all of the inputs. A
typical PDH system allowed a 50 PPM plus or minus variation in the rate of the
inputs, which means that the output had to be at least 50 PPM fast relative to
the sum of the inputs. That way, the multiplexer will never "fall behind"
because an input is providing bits faster than the output can interleave them.

The other thing to know is that the multiplexer must perform a function known as
either stuffing or justification. It is said that the term justification
was introduced within AT&T because it sounded more technical, while stuffing
was more popular with the actual engineers. Certain parts of each outgoing frame
are defined (by standard) as stuffable, and they're sometimes called gaps.
These are sections where the multiplexer is allowed to either include real data,
or to include some nonsense data called stuffing bits (or, if you want to
sound more technical, justification bits). By choosing to either include real
data or stuffing in the gaps, the multiplexer can actually adjust the "real"
output data rate up or down. That way, it converges onto the correct average
(the sum of the inputs) despite the "timing noise" of the inputs varying
slightly up and down in real speed.

If that didn't make sense to you, here's a different way to think about the same
thing: we can imagine the DS2 output frame as consisting of four "slots" into
which the four DS1 input frames are inserted (this isn't quite intuitive because
they are interleaved bit-by-bit, but the math works out the same). Under the PDH
design, these slots are all slightly wider than the input frames, so that
there is "free space" for the input frames to be shifted a bit in either
direction or stretched out. That allows the multiplexer to "catch up" on a fast
input or to "draw out" the frames from a slow input. Thinking about it in terms
of a wide slot that you can place the input into as desired also gives more
value to the term "justification:" you can shift bits around, or add extra space
in between them, just like you would to justify text.

The actual implementation of this idea is pretty complicated, because the
demultiplexer on the other end needs to know which bits were stuffed so that
they can be discarded. That's why PDH specified gaps at fixed positions: the
control signaling included a set of flags that indicated whether the fixed gaps
were used for data or stuffing. When the multiplexer decided whether or not to
use a stuffable bit (based on whether or not the input was getting ahead of the
output mux), it also had to store that decision for the end of the frame so that
the flag could be set correctly.

PDH wasn't an elegant solution, but it was a solution, and multiplexers were
designed up to the DS4 level based on the PDH approach. We all owe PDH a huge
thanks for providing the clunky stopgap that allowed the construction of a
nationwide digital telephone network. That said, well, it had quite a few
downsides.

First, PDH was never all that well standardized. Researching PDH is tricky
because there aren't a lot of documents that provide conclusive detail about the
actual implementation in the US, mostly just summaries, conceptual sketches, and
examples from Europe. As far as I can tell 2, Western Electric never really
offered a standalone PDH multiplexer. Larger integrated systems from Western
Electric (like, say, a microwave carrier equipment bay) might include a PDH
multiplexer, but it's not clear to me if WE even made them—the advertisements
and pricing information I can find for PDH multiplexers are from other vendors
like Farinon and NEC.

In North American practice, it doesn't seem like PDH was ever robustly
standardized, and there were implementation differences between equipment from
different manufacturers. That's probably one of the reasons for the scarcity of
information on PDH equipment: you wouldn't usually buy a single PDH multiplexer,
but instead would specify a specific model as part of a larger system. That
meant that the PDH network was far less flexible than AT&T had hoped.

The problem was even bigger when you looked overseas: AT&T tended to field
the best thing that Bell Labs and Western Electric could come up with, and then
promulgate that as a standard later on. The European telcos tended not to adopt
new American developments until they were mature, giving them the opportunity to
make standards before any equipment was in place. Thus the European versions of
US telephone carriers are often a bit better, and PDH is no exception. In fact,
the US, Europe, and Japan used three different hierarchies for PDH signaling.
The European standard put more channels into a stream (the "E1" at about 2
Mbps), and used a consistent multiplier of 4 for each level. European PDH
practices even got a complete published standard from CCITT. The Japanese system
used the same DS1 standard as the US but with different multipliers (4, 5, 3, 4
instead of 4, 7, 6). PDH could thus not be used for international calling
without completely remuxing everything.

Another shortcoming of PDH had to do with that remuxing. The decision to
bit-interleave the input frames together, stuff some bits, and then put flags on
the bit stuffing into the interleaved stream, meant that a PDH multiplexer
effectively "scrambled" the input streams. If you had, say, a DS3 stream and
wanted to extract a single voice channel from it, you had a lot of work in front
of you. It simply wasn't feasible with the electronics of the era to analyze the
stream to determine the interleaving and stuffing bits at each level. Instead,
you would have to put the DS3 through demuxers all the way back down to the
bottom of the hierarchy, pull out the channel you wanted, and then remux it all
the way back up. Pulling a single channel out of a DS3 could require two 11.5
foot tall equipment bays, and even further quantization noise due to the nature
of the robbed bit scheme.

Two things happened that pushed PDH to its limit: first, fiber optics. AT&T was
famously a late adopter of fiber, and 1970s documents on the digital hierarchy
talked about conveying it over T-carrier, microwave, and coaxial. We have
talked about coaxial
before, but L-carrier
was an analog system. Digital coaxial did emerge as the T3, T4, and T5 carriers,
but these were relatively short range and mostly only saw use on shorter
inter-office links.

Things were changing, though: by the time DS3 equipment was appearing in
telephone exchanges, competitors were already evaluating fiber optics. AT&T
dipped their toe in the water in 1976, with an experimental DS3 fiber optic link
in Atlanta. The next year, both AT&T and competitor GTE had DS3 fiber lines in
service (in Chicago and the LA area, respectively). Outside manufacturers
started offering T1-over-fiber equipment around 1980, and in 1983 AT&T had a
multimode fiber system stretching from New York to Washington. Sparing the
(fascinating) story of the business and competitive factors, the writing was on
the wall: fiber was the future of long lines. AT&T engineers realized that the
PDH design did not scale well to the enormous capacities that fiber could reach,
and even worse, that complex fiber networks would require exactly the capability
that PDH lacked: extracting single channels from the mux. Besides, despite the
systems in use, there really wasn't any standard for conveying PDH signals over
fiber, which only meant more compatibility issues.

Something else was coming over the horizon in 1983: divestiture. The complete
reorganization of AT&T in the mid-1980s, breaking the Baby Bells up into
independent companies, made the interoperability problems with PDH much more
severe. Bell operating companies (BOCs) would need to easily exchange traffic
with both AT&T Long Lines and, eventually, with other BOCs and competitive
phone companies and long distance carriers. That was very difficult when that
traffic was mostly conveyed in loosely-standardized black-box muxes. Many
aspects of US telephony were loosely standardized prior to the Bell System
breakup because AT&T ran the entire network and didn't really need to cooperate
with others. After 1984, the US became a lot more like Europe: for technology to
be widely adopted, it would need to have a well-defined, published standard.

That meant a standards body—the part of AT&T that had formerly published the
practices used by all of the BOCs, after divestiture, became an independent
company called Bellcore. Bellcore had an immediate goal of developing a fully
standardized set of digital interfaces to be used between telephone companies.
At the same time, a group of carriers and equipment manufacturers organized an
association to start an ANSI standards process for fiber-optic equipment. They
had a goal of an industry standard for high-speed digital fiber optics, so that
terminal equipment from different manufacturers could be used together.

That effort formed the ANSI T1X1 working group, titled Digital Hierarchy and
Synchronization. In 1985, Bellcore proposed their draft standard to the T1X1
committee: they called it SONET.
Synchronicity

First, I will briefly explain some context for my global readers. One of the
shortcomings of PDH was its lack of international standardization, and SONET
would not make the same mistake. Shortly after SONET was proposed to ANSI, it
was also proposed to CCITT. For historic reasons, and despite the fact that they
are largely identical, SONET (Synchronous Optical Network) is a North American
standard while the European standard is called SDH, for Synchronous Digital
Hierarchy. I will stick to the term SONET because it is catchier, but the name
SDH better conveys that SONET is essentially the same idea as PDH but it's
actually synchronous. Beyond that, it is also more feature-rich and much better
standardized.

SONET starts out higher up in the digital hierarchy. The "lowest" SONET level
is Synchronous Transport Signal 1, or STS-1, which is typically transported by
Optical Carrier 1, or OC-1. OC-1 operates at 51.84 Mbps, sufficient to carry a
PDH DS3 channel with signaling overhead. By this point in telecommunications
history, channel banks had improved and 50 Mbps wasn't what it once was, so
DS3 was a good choice for the basic unit of a high-capacity transport system.
This also provided critical backwards compatibility: DS3 was the most widely
deployed PDH signal, so by accommodating a DS3 within an STS-1, SONET provided an
easy route to tunneling legacy PDH links through a SONET replacement.

I put a lot of time into writing this, and I hope that you enjoy reading
it. If you can spare a few dollars, consider supporting me on
ko-fi. You'll receive an occasional extra,
subscribers-only post, and defray the costs of providing artisanal, hand-built
world wide web directly from Albuquerque, New Mexico.

By this time, the Digital Hierarchy principle from PDH was well established, so
SONET follows the exact same pattern—but, fortunately, the naming convention
improved. OC-3 is three times the bandwidth of OC-1, OC-12 is twelve times the
bandwidth of OC-1, and so on, with OC-24, OC-48, OC-192, and even OC-768 in
common use, the latter achieving over 38 Gbps of payload.

SONET is complex compared to what you might expect, or at least different. A
SONET frame does not consist of a header and a body. Instead, like with PDH, all
of the data is interleaved together in a way that feels messy. In an STS-1
signal, for example, a frame consists of three bytes of protocol overhead and
87 bytes of payload, making up a 90 byte pattern that is repeated nine times to
make up an 810 byte frame. Higher levels use larger frames but keep the same
structure, effectively mixing the header into each frame. Like PDH's bitwise
interleaving, this is done to manage latency: interleaving the header with the
payload avoids the need to buffer an entire frame of data at any point. Because
of this design decision, SONET can provide a latency that is less than the frame
time.

This description also oversimplifies by discussing only one part of SONET's
protocol overhead. There are actually several layers of overhead, all
interleaved together, that serve different purposes. The "lowest layer" overhead
is recreated at each regenerator along the route (devices that decode and then
reencode the optical signaling to compensate for path loss), while higher layers
are only processed by terminal equipment and are used for purposes like
connection quality monitoring.

These types of overhead are important because, unlike PDH, SONET provides a
specification for the entire physical infrastructure. SONET is virtually always
used with one of a few standard architectures, each of which are designed to
provide redundancy. SONET uses unidirectional signaling on the fiber, so any
SONET link will have two fibers normally active, one for each direction. Where
things vary are the approach to redundancy: in a linear route with automatic
protection, there are two "spare" fibers. When terminal equipment detects (via
monitoring protocol overhead signaling) that the connection quality is no longer
good on the primary pair of fibers, it will switch automatically to the
secondary pair.

Particularly common with SONET though, and particularly distinctive, are rings.
A unidirectional ring uses two fibers, one for each direction, but each of those
fibers goes in a circle and returns to the origin point. At the origin point,
each frame is transmitted both directions into the ring. The terminals
elsewhere on the ring compare the two copies that they received, one from each
direction, and use the better of the two. This provides protection against
damage to one of the fibers: terminals that are "downstream" from a broken fiber
should still be able to receive the frames that went the other way around.

A downside to this protection method is that it is inefficient: sending every
frame twice means that two fibers are still providing a theoretical maximum
bandwidth equal to the capacity of a single fiber. Bidirectional rings use a
more complicated monitoring scheme to detect when frames are lost, so that they
do not need to preemptively send them twice. A broken fiber will be detected
and, depending on the ring, either sent the other way around or sent on a second
redundant fiber allocated to the same direction.

SONET's ring architecture is one of its most interesting properties.
Unidirectional rings are often used as the "last mile" component of a SONET
network. Consider, for example, a large business in the early days of the
internet. If you wanted 100 Mbps internet connectivity, one of your best options
was to purchase SONET service from the telephone company. They would take an
existing ring, starting and ending with a telephone exchange, and figure out
how to add your premises somewhere along it. The ring shape allowed redundancy
with a relatively efficient use of fiber length.

Bidirectional rings, with their greater complexity but greater efficiency, were
usually used between telephone exchanges where there was adequate room for more
complex terminal equipment.

The ring topology also illustrates the biggest advantage of SONET over PDH.
Unlike PDH, SONET hierarchy levels keep overhead and frame data in the same
position, with consistent offsets to the framing data necessary to find an
individual channel. That means that it is practical to inspect a high-rate SONET
link, find a specific channel, and pull out those bits. You can even find where
a channel is located and then overwrite just those bits, inserting data into the
stream. This pattern is called "add-drop multiplexing," because the multiplexer
usually adds some channels and drops others.

Let's work a concrete example. Many years ago, I was an intern at a General
Electric plant in Virginia. Although the facility's main internet connectivity
had since been upgraded, SONET service was still active for redundancy and for a
legacy TDM PABX. In an equipment room, the telco-owned add-drop multiplexer sat
in a rack with the fiber enclosures where the building was actually spliced into
the ring. The multiplexer was the customer premises equipment, and our Cisco
router was connected by OC fiber to the multiplexer's "low speed" side while its
"high speed" side had two connections, one each way, to our "neighbors" on the
ring. The telco had left a diagram taped to the rack that made this material:
one pair of fibers went to the National Radio Astronomy Observatory, the other
went to the National Geospatial Intelligence Agency. There must have been some
interesting traffic on that ring!

The multiplexer found the time slots in the SONET ring that were assigned to
us, "dropped" them and sent those bits out on the low-speed side, and then
received bits on the low-speed side that were "added" back into the same time
slots. Each of the organizations along the ring did the same thing with their
own channels.

The fact that the SONET ring had to "pass through" each of its users was a
material downside, since a failure of an add-drop multiplexer at one customer
could cause service disruptions for others. That's why the multiplexer was
telco property, and further why SONET rings were always deployed with some type
of automatic protection and redundancy. Ultimately, though, a telephone company
technician still showed up at the security desk from time to time, needing to
perform maintenance or repairs on the SONET equipment.

The ability to perform add-drop multiplexing at any point on a SONET link also
enabled digital cross-connects. This, finally, was the original dream of the
nationwide digital network: by pairing two add-drop multiplexers together, you
can switch channels from one SONET line onto another, completely digitally and
with almost no latency. Paired with a management protocol called Transaction
language 1 (TL1) for remote reconfiguration, digital cross connects make the
long distance network vastly more flexible. Big chunks of long distance traffic
could be instantly rerouted, and consolidated onto major routes or spread across
more minor ones.

Now, you might wonder, what happened to the whole synchronization problem? The
most obvious difference between PDH and SONET is that PDH is plesiochronous
while SONET is synchronous. SONET requires that all of the terminals, at least
within a given interconnected network, operate in synchronization. That's
exactly the requirement that PDH rejected. What changed is the state of the art
in timing and synchronization.

A few things came together to obsolete the need for plesiochronous technology.
One was the introduction of the Bell System Reference Frequency: to coordinate
both analog and digital systems that were timing-sensitive, AT&T introduced a
nationwide time synchronization system. By the 1980s, the 2048 kHz Bell System
Reference Frequency was distributed to nearly all telephone facilities over the
long distance infrastructure. Various time code systems followed. During the
same period, GPS was coming online, and GPS receivers became a relatively
inexpensive source of precise time.

Most terminals on a SONET ring got their timing from the ring: they just
followed the signal and added or dropped channels at the appropriate time. A
"master" terminal, typically at the telephone exchange, had to maintain that
beat. In the early days, it would likely derive its clock either from an atomic
clock in the office or via a reference signal coming from another office. In the
later days of SONET, the time source was more likely to be a "BITS" or Building
Integrated Timing Supply. BITS are basically time servers for telephone offices,
typically using a GPS receiver as their discipline source and transmitting a few
different types of TDM time codes to whatever devices needed them.

Despite all of these measures, it's interesting that SONET still cheats. There
is a bit of wiggle room. Part of the SONET protocol overhead is a pointer that
indicates the offset within the frame that the payload frame actually starts.
SONET devices can thus start the payload a little bit late in a SONET frame,
providing an opportunity to fix timing errors. This capability means that SONET
is still an option even in plesiochronous environments, which eased the fairly
rapid transition from PDH to SONET.
SONET in Use

SONET is fast enough to survive into the modern era, although it is now
decidedly legacy. 38 Gbps is nothing to sneeze at, and still compares favorably
with a lot of common long distance connections. Where SONET shows its age is in
the actual network payload. What do you actually put on a SONET ring?

Well, of course, you can fit a whole lot of 64 Kbps telephone channels onto any
of the SONET tiers. You can do that using a "raw" T1 signal or via ISDN, which
uses the same basic fiber signals but better standardizes telephone signaling
(e.g. off hook status) and interoperability. But even an OC-1 has 672 channels,
more phone calls than just about anyone needs to make. In the 1980s, the driver
for commercial SONET service was data.

SONET itself is incredibly protocol neutral—one of the reasons for its unusual
framing structure is that it is agnostic to the size, rate, and timing of the
frames of the next layer protocol. SONET basically treats all connections as
opaque serial streams, so conceptually, you can put just about anything over it.

Because SONET evolved during the same period as ISDN, the two are closely
related. During the late '80s, as SONET was being deployed, the "Broadband ISDN"
initiative created Asynchronous Transfer Mode (ATM). ATM is a virtual circuit
switching protocol that multiplexes a large number of small, fixed-size packets
(called cells) over high-speed connections like SONET. ATM was, at one time, a
serious contender for the dominant protocol in wide area networks. That didn't
come to be, though, and IP took over—but not before ATM was well-enough
established to be a tempting way to carry IP. IP over ATM was fairly common, and
in fact, remained the norm for DSL until fairly recently.

There were other options as well: Packet over SONET was a standard for
SONET-based PPP connections, which could carry just about anything but were
often used for IP. A newer offering is Ethernet over SONET, which does exactly
what it sounds like.

The internet provided a compelling use-case for SONET, but it also became a
challenge. SONET was designed within the telephone industry, which emphasized
handling fixed-speed channels with very high reliability and very low latency.
The IP-based internet embraced the opposite: opportunistically moving variable
speed connections over relatively high-latency and low-reliability channels.
That meant that internet service over SONET became awkward.

For one, it tended to be slow. The reason was bandwidth allocation: getting time
on a SONET ring means getting channels assigned, and you will pay for those
channels 24/7 regardless of whether or not you use them. A technology called
virtual concatenation was developed to allow SONET's lower-level building blocks
(like STS-1) to be combined in arbitrary ways to produce just about any amount
of bandwidth you could want, but every Mbps over SONET was an Mbps that couldn't
be used by any other customer. You paid for it. Later on, variable-bandwidth
allocation systems were developed, but they were complex and missed the
opportunity to make much of a difference.

SONET's fixed-bandwidth design made it excellent for real-time media, the
wheelhouse of the telephone industry, but ironically real-time media was missing
from the information revolution. Internet connections were generally too slow
and unreliable to carry it. By the time real-time media returned, IP connections
had gotten so fast that they could make up for the lack of traffic engineering
with raw speed. Slow and reliable lost out to fast and unreliable almost every
time.

SONET also had all the typical warts of a telephone industry network
architecture. By the '90s, IP-based network equipment was both cheaper and
easier to use than ATM and SONET devices. Upstart internet service providers
were much more competitively motivated, driving down prices on non-SONET
services.

SONET has been superseded as a standard by OTN, Optical
Transport Network. OTN is an ITU standard for a digital hierarchy that starts at
2.5 Gbps and goes up, well, as high as you want. 800 Gbps "OTUC8" is now in
service. Besides being faster, OTN is also designed to accommodate variable
packet connections like Ethernet much more efficiently. And, of course, even OTN
is losing the fight against schemes that carry Ethernet frames directly over
fiber.

Is this the reason that 8-bit bytes became so universal in computing? I
genuinely do not know, this would be a good topic for future research. A long
time ago, on a different blog, I spent some time trying to establish the lineage
of the 8-bit word length that is now so universal. Without devoting a career of
research to the topic, I think the best I can say is that there seem to have
been several parallel paths that converged on 7 and 8 bits as good choices
for communications purposes. Digital telephony equipment was certainly one of
them.↩
